docs.title: 🎯 Probability Distributions
docs.text:
Probability refers to the chance or likelihood of a particular event taking place. It is a pure number ranging between 0 and 1.

Probability Distribution is the total listing of the various values a random variable can take along with the corresponding probability of each value.

Probability distributions can be broadly classified into two main categories:

  • Discrete Probability Distributions: Deal with countable outcomes
  • Continuous Probability Distributions: Deal with uncountable outcomes over intervals

docs.title: Conditional Probability
docs.text:
Conditional Probability is the probability of an event occurring, which depends on the occurrence of another event. The two events are dependent on each other.

Formula:

P(B|A) = P(A∩B) / P(A)

Where: - P(B|A) is the conditional probability of event B occurring, given that event A has already occurred - P(A∩B) is the probability of both events A and B occurring simultaneously - P(A) is the probability of event A occurring

Example: From a pack of 52 cards, if you randomly select a card and it is a black card, the probability that the card is a spade is 13/26 = 1/2.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 📊 Statistical Inference
docs.text: Statistical inference comprises gathering knowledge about a population through a random sample. Since a population is completely known through its parameters, the problem reduces to assessing population parameters through sample statistics.

docs.title: Key Definitions
docs.text:
Population: The largest possible collection of items with a set of common characteristics. Size denoted by N (may be finite or infinite).

Sample: A subset of the population. Size denoted by n (always finite).

Random Sample: A subset where each unit of the population has an equal chance of selection.

Population Parameter: Constants that determine a population (e.g., μ, σ², π). Typically denoted by Greek letters.

Sample Statistic: Quantities derived from the sample (e.g., x̅, x̃, s). Denoted by Roman letters.

docs.title: Illustrative Example
docs.text:
Population of size N = 5: [8, 3, 9, 0, 4], Population mean = 4.8

  • Sample 1 (n = 3): [8, 0, 4], Sample average = 4.0
  • Sample 2 (n = 3): [3, 4, 9], Sample average = 5.33

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 🔍 Hypothesis Testing
docs.text: Hypothesis testing is a statistical method to determine whether there is enough evidence to reject a claim about a population parameter.

docs.title: Core Components
docs.text:
Null Hypothesis (H₀): The assumption that there is no significant difference or effect.

Alternative Hypothesis (Hₐ): The claim that contradicts the null hypothesis.

Significance Level (α): The probability threshold (commonly 0.05) for rejecting H₀.

Test Statistic: A standardized value used to decide whether to reject H₀.

docs.title: Z-Statistic Formula
docs.text: Z = (sample mean - population mean) / (population standard deviation / √n)

docs.title: Key Terms
docs.text:
• Type I Error (α): Rejecting H₀ when it should not be rejected
  • Type II Error (β): Failing to reject H₀ when it should be rejected
  • P-value: The actual risk level calculated from the data
  • Confidence Level: How confident we are in our decision (typically 95%)
  • Confidence Interval: Range of values expected to contain the true parameter

Confidence Interval Formula:

CI = X̅ ± Z × (σ/√n)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 📈 Logistic Regression
docs.text: Logistic Regression is a statistical model used for binary classification problems. It predicts the probability that an observation belongs to one of two possible classes.

docs.title: Why Not Linear Regression for Classification?
docs.text: Linear regression has several limitations for classification: - Outputs are not bounded between 0 and 1 - Cannot be interpreted as probabilities - Sensitive to outliers - Decision boundary changes with new data points

docs.title: The Logistic Regression Model
docs.text:
The model uses the sigmoid function to map any real value to a value between 0 and 1:

Sigmoid Function:

h_θ(x) = 1 / (1 + e^(-z))

Where z = θᵀX = θ₀ + θ₁x₁ + θ₂x₂ + ...

docs.title: Prediction Rules
docs.text:
• ŷ = 1 if h(X) > 0.5
  • ŷ = 0 if h(X) < 0.5

docs.title: Advantages
docs.text:
1. Simplicity: Easy to implement with great training efficiency
  2. Interpretability: Provides probabilistic outputs
  3. Linear Separability: Works well when data is linearly separable

docs.title: Assumptions
docs.text:
1. Binary dependent variable: Target must be categorical and binary
  2. Independence: Observations must be independent
  3. Low multicollinearity: Independent variables shouldn't be highly correlated

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: ⚡ Support Vector Machines
docs.text: Support Vector Machine (SVM) is a supervised learning algorithm for classification and regression. The main objective is to find the optimal hyperplane that separates classes with maximum margin.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
Support Vectors: Data points closest to the decision boundary.

Margin: Distance between the hyperplane and the nearest support vectors.

Hyperplane: Decision boundary that separates classes.

docs.title: Types of Margins
docs.text:
Hard Margin: - No misclassification allowed - All data points correctly classified - Sensitive to outliers - Works only for perfectly separable data

Soft Margin: - Allows some misclassification - Balances margin maximization with error minimization - Robust to outliers - Better generalization

docs.title: Non-linear SVM and Kernel Trick
docs.text: For non-linearly separable data, SVM uses the kernel trick to transform data into higher dimensions where it becomes linearly separable.

docs.title: Common Kernel Functions
docs.text:
1. Polynomial Kernel:

K(xi, xj) = (γ⟨xi, xj⟩ + r)^d

2. Radial Basis Function (RBF) Kernel:

K(xi, xj) = exp(-γ||xi - xj||²)

docs.title: Gamma Parameter in RBF
docs.text:
• Small γ: Wider influence, smoother boundary (potential underfitting)
  • Large γ: Narrow influence, complex boundary (potential overfitting)

docs.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text:
Advantages: - Flexible with different data types - Kernel functions handle complexity well - Less prone to overfitting

Disadvantages: - High training time for large datasets - Difficult interpretability (black-box approach)

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 🌳 Decision Trees
docs.text: Decision trees are tree-based models that make decisions through a hierarchical structure, splitting datasets into smaller subsets based on feature values.

docs.title: Key Concepts
docs.text:
Entropy: Measure of randomness or impurity in a dataset.

H(Y) = -Σ pi log₂(pi)

Information Gain: Measure of information gained by adding a feature.

Information Gain = H(Y) - H(Y|X)

docs.title: Important Terminology
docs.text:
• Root Node: Starting point of the decision tree
  • Branch/Sub-Tree: Part of the entire decision tree
  • Splitting: Dividing a node based on conditions
  • Decision Node: Node that splits into further sub-nodes
  • Leaf/Terminal Node: End node that cannot be split further
  • Depth: Number of levels from root to furthest leaf

docs.title: Tree Construction Process
docs.text:
1. Calculate entropy for the target variable
  2. Calculate information gain for each feature
  3. Select feature with highest information gain as root
  4. Split data based on selected feature
  5. Repeat recursively for each branch
  6. Stop when nodes become pure or stopping criteria met

docs.title: Tree Pruning
docs.text:
Pruning reduces overfitting by removing parts of the tree that provide little predictive power.

Benefits: - Reduces overfitting - Improves generalization - Simplifies model structure - May slightly increase training error but decreases testing error

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 🎯 Ensemble Methods
docs.text: Ensemble methods combine multiple models to create a stronger predictor than individual models alone.

docs.title: Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregation)
docs.text: Process: 1. Create multiple bootstrap samples from original dataset 2. Train base model on each sample 3. Aggregate predictions (voting for classification, averaging for regression)

docs.title: Random Forest
docs.text:
Random Forest extends bagging by using decision trees as base models and introducing additional randomness through feature selection.

Key Features: - Uses bootstrap sampling - Considers random subset of features at each split - Combines multiple decision trees - Reduces overfitting compared to individual trees

For Classification: Uses majority voting For Regression: Uses average of predictions

Advantages: - Handles overfitting well - Works with both numerical and categorical data - Provides feature importance measures - Robust to outliers and noise

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: 🎯 K-Nearest Neighbors
docs.text: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) is a lazy learning algorithm that classifies data points based on the class of their k nearest neighbors in the feature space.

docs.title: Algorithm Steps
docs.text:
1. Choose the number K of neighbors
  2. Calculate Euclidean distance to all training points
  3. Select K nearest neighbors
  4. Count class frequency among neighbors
  5. Assign class with highest frequency
  6. Model ready for predictions

docs.title: Distance Calculation
docs.text:
Euclidean Distance:

d = √[(x₁-y₁)² + (x₂-y₂)² + ... + (xₙ-yₙ)²]

docs.title: Choosing K Value
docs.text:
• Small K (1-2): Can be noisy, sensitive to outliers
  • Large K: More stable but may lose local patterns
  • Rule of thumb: K = √n (where n is number of training samples)
  • Cross-validation: Best method to determine optimal K

docs.title: Characteristics
docs.text: Properties: - Lazy Learning: No specialized training phase - Non-parametric: Makes no assumptions about data distribution - Instance-based: Uses all data for classification

docs.title: Advantages and Disadvantages
docs.text:
Advantages: - Simple to understand and implement - No assumptions about data distribution - Works well with small datasets - Can be used for both classification and regression

Disadvantages: - Computationally expensive for large datasets - Sensitive to irrelevant features - Requires feature scaling - Performance depends heavily on K choice

↩ Back to Top

docs.text: Algorithm Type Strengths Weaknesses Best Use Case Logistic Regression Linear Simple, interpretable, fast Assumes linear relationship Binary classification, baseline model SVM Linear/Non-linear Effective in high dimensions, memory efficient Slow on large datasets Text classification, high-dimensional data Decision Trees Non-linear Easy to interpret, handles mixed data types Prone to overfitting Feature selection, interpretable models Random Forest Ensemble Reduces overfitting, feature importance Less interpretable than single tree General-purpose classification/regression KNN Instance-based Simple, no assumptions Computationally expensive Small datasets, non-linear patterns

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
The discovery of DNA and its role in storing biological information revolutionized biology. DNA, represented using the alphabet A, C, G, and T, encodes genetic instructions through sequences called codons. This study demonstrates how unsupervised learning techniques, specifically PCA and K-Means clustering, can reveal the codon structure in bacterial DNA without prior labeling.

The focus is on the genomic sequence of Caulobacter Crescentus, revealing the underlying 3-letter codon structure using data science methods.

docs.title: 2. Dataset Description
docs.text:
• Source: DNA sequence fragment of Caulobacter Crescentus
  • File format: .fa (FASTA format)
  • Size: ~300,000 base pairs
  • Structure: Continuous string of A, C, G, T without spaces
  • Processing:
  • Sequence split into non-overlapping 300 bp segments
  • Generated frequency tables for word lengths \( M = 1, 2, 3, 4 \)
  • Features: \( 4^M \) for each M

docs.title: 3. Methodology
docs.text:
1. Sequence Segmentation:
  2. Break sequence into fixed-length substrings.
  3. Feature Extraction:
  4. For each \( M \), count occurrences of each possible word (e.g., for \( M=2 \), 16 features).
  5. Normalization:
  6. Standardize each feature by subtracting the mean and dividing by standard deviation.
  7. Dimensionality Reduction:
  8. Apply PCA to visualize patterns.
  9. Clustering:
  10. Apply K-Means in the high-dimensional space, then visualize results in PCA-reduced space.

docs.title: 4. Python Implementation
docs.text:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
import pandas as pd

pca = PCA(n_components=2)
pCompTables = {}

for i in range(1,5):
    pca.fit(normFreqTables[i])
    pCompTables[i] = pd.DataFrame(
        pca.transform(normFreqTables[i])[:, 0:2], 
        columns=['pc1', 'pc2']
    )
    print(f'Explained variance for {i} letters: {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum()}')

print(pCompTables[2].head())

  • For \( M=3 \): Clear structure emerges, with six lobes (3 reading frames forward, 3 backward) and a central blob representing non-coding regions.
  • Codons are confirmed as 3-letter words, encoding amino acids.

docs.title: 6.Understanding PC1 and PC2 in PCA
docs.text:
When performing Principal Component Analysis (PCA), the goal is to reduce high-dimensional data into a smaller set of dimensions while retaining as much of the variation (information) as possible.

In this example, we use:

pca = PCA(n_components=2)

This means we are projecting our data onto two new orthogonal axes:

  • PC1 (Principal Component 1) → Captures the largest variance in the data.
  • PC2 (Principal Component 2) → Captures the second-largest variance, orthogonal to PC1.

By keeping only 2 components, we can:

  1. Visualize the data in a 2D plot (PC1 vs PC2).
  2. Preserve most of the important variation while removing noise.

docs.title: Python Example
docs.text:
pca = PCA(n_components=2)

pCompTables = {}

for i in range(1,5):
    pca.fit(normFreqTables[i])
    pComponents = pca.transform(normFreqTables[i])
    # for each word size, store only PC1 and PC2 in a DataFrame
    pCompTables[i] = pd.DataFrame(pComponents[:, [0,1]], columns = ['pc1', 'pc2'])
    print('Explained variance for ' + str(i) + ' letters: ' + str(pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum()))

print(pCompTables[2].head())

Explained variance for 2 letters: 0.22774966356188592
Explained variance for 3 letters: 0.31670201938180154
Explained variance for 4 letters: 0.029334525098408036

docs.title: Why PC1 and PC2?
docs.text:
• PC1: Finds the direction in the dataset that explains the most variance.
  • PC2: Finds the next most informative direction, constrained to be orthogonal to PC1.
  • By choosing 2 components, we balance interpretability and variance preservation.
  • These components are often used for visualizing high-dimensional data in 2D.

docs.text:
• Validates biological discovery of codons using purely computational unsupervised methods.
  • Demonstrates applicability of ML in genomics.
  • Provides a workflow adaptable to other genomic datasets.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text: This case study demonstrates Principal Component Analysis (PCA) applied to the Auto MPG dataset to reduce feature dimensionality while retaining most of the variance in the dataset.

docs.title: 2. Dataset Description

docs.text:
1. Standardize features using StandardScaler.
  2. Apply PCA to transform features into uncorrelated principal components.
  3. Analyze explained variance to decide number of components to keep.
  4. Interpret PC1 and PC2 loadings to understand meaning.

docs.title: 4. Python Implementation

docs.title: Cumulative Explained Variance
docs.text:
• PC1 explains ~73% of variance.
  • PC1 + PC2 explain ~91%.
  • After PC2, returns diminish — so PC1 & PC2 are enough for most analyses.

docs.title: Principal Component Equations
docs.text:
PC1: [ PC1 = -0.40 \cdot mpg + 0.42 \cdot cylinders + 0.43 \cdot displacement + 0.42 \cdot horsepower + 0.41 \cdot weight - 0.28 \cdot acceleration - 0.23 \cdot model_year ] Interpretation: Large engines (high cylinders, displacement, horsepower, weight) with low mpg.

PC2: Dominated by negative weight on model_year. Separates older cars from newer cars.

PC3: Mainly acceleration — less important.

docs.title: 6. Use Case Impact
docs.text:
• PC1 & PC2 can visualize clusters (e.g., sports cars vs. economy cars).
  • Dimensionality reduction helps in clustering and visualization while keeping most dataset information.

docs.title: 7. How to Read PCA Component Loadings
docs.text:
When interpreting PCA results, each principal component (PC) is expressed as a linear combination of the original features, with a numerical weight (loading) assigned to each feature.

  • Sign of the loading:
  • A positive loading means that as the principal component’s value increases, the original feature tends to increase.

  • A negative loading means that as the principal component’s value increases, the original feature tends to decrease.

  • Magnitude of the loading:

  • The larger the absolute value of a loading, the more influence that feature has on that principal component.

  • For example, a weight of 0.45 contributes more strongly than 0.10.

  • Example reading of PC1: If PC1 is [ -0.40 \cdot mpg + 0.42 \cdot cylinders + 0.43 \cdot displacement + 0.42 \cdot horsepower + 0.41 \cdot weight - 0.28 \cdot acceleration - 0.23 \cdot model\ year ]

  • The largest positive loadings (e.g., cylinders, displacement, horsepower, weight) suggest PC1 increases with bigger, more powerful, heavier cars.
  • The largest negative loading (mpg) means higher PC1 scores correspond to lower fuel efficiency.

  • Interpretation: PC1 captures the “heavy engine, low mileage” profile.

  • Explained Variance Ratio:

  • Each PC also has a percentage that shows how much of the dataset’s variance it explains.
  • For example, PC1 might explain 70% of the variance, meaning it captures most of the patterns in the data.

✅ In summary: Look for the largest absolute loadings in each PC to understand which features dominate that component. Signs tell you the direction of influence, magnitudes tell you the strength, and the explained variance tells you the importance of the component.

docs.title: 🎯 Overview
docs.text: Modularity Clustering is a powerful unsupervised method for detecting communities in network graphs that automatically determines the optimal number of communities without requiring prior specification. Unlike spectral clustering methods that need predefined cluster counts, modularity clustering maximizes a quality metric called the modularity score to identify natural community structures.

docs.title: Key Advantages
docs.text:
• 🔄 Automatic cluster detection - No need to specify number of communities
  • 📊 Quality-driven - Uses modularity score optimization
  • 🌐 Widely applicable - Works across various network types
  • ⚖️ Baseline comparison - Compares against random network models

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Community Quality Measurement
docs.text: The fundamental idea behind modularity clustering is to identify communities that have significantly more internal connections than would be expected in a random baseline graph with similar properties.

docs.title: The Baseline Principle
docs.text:
Good communities should have:

  • High internal connectivity - Many edges within the community
  • Significant deviation from random - More connections than baseline expectation
  • Clear boundaries - Fewer connections to other communities

docs.title: Modularity Score Interpretation
docs.text:
Score Range Interpretation Community Quality Q > 0.7 Excellent Very strong community structure 0.4 - 0.7 Good Clear community boundaries 0.1 - 0.4 Moderate Weak but detectable structure Q ≈ 0 Random No significant community structure Q < 0 Anti-community Fewer internal edges than expected

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Mathematical Foundation
docs.text:
The modularity score for a given partitioning is calculated as:

\[Q = \sum_{i,j \text{ in same community}} (A_{ij} - P_{ij})\]

Where: - Aij = 1 if there's an edge between nodes i and j, 0 otherwise - Pij = Expected number of edges between i and j in baseline graph

docs.title: Normalized Modularity
docs.text:
The complete modularity formula includes normalization:

\[Q = \frac{1}{2m} \sum_{i,j} \left[ A_{ij} - \frac{k_i k_j}{2m} \right] \delta(c_i, c_j)\]

Where: - m = Total number of edges in the graph - ki = Degree of node i - δ(ci, cj) = 1 if nodes i and j are in the same community, 0 otherwise

docs.title: Community-Level Calculation
docs.text:
For multiple communities, the total modularity is:

\[Q = \sum_{communities} \left( \frac{\text{edges in community}}{\text{total edges}} - \left(\frac{\text{total degree in community}}{2 \times \text{total edges}}\right)^2 \right)\]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Expected Edge Probability
docs.text:
The baseline model calculates the expected probability of an edge between nodes i and j:

\[P_{ij} = \frac{\text{degree}(i) \times \text{degree}(j)}{2 \times \text{total edges}}\]

docs.title: Configuration Model Properties
docs.text:
The baseline (configuration) model preserves:

  • ✅ Total number of edges
  • ✅ Degree sequence of all nodes
  • ✅ Graph density
  • ❌ Specific edge arrangements (randomized)

docs.title: Example Calculation
docs.text:
For a node with degree 3 connected to another node with degree 3 in a graph with 17 total edges:

\[P_{ij} = \frac{3 \times 3}{2 \times 17} = \frac{9}{34} ≈ 26\%\]

This means there's a 26% chance these nodes would be connected in the baseline model.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Matrix Construction
docs.text:
Modularity clustering uses eigenvector analysis on the modularity matrix B:

\[B_{ij} = A_{ij} - \frac{k_i k_j}{2m}\]

docs.title: Eigenvector Analysis Steps
docs.text:
1. Construct modularity matrix B with entries (Aij - Pij)
  2. Calculate eigenvectors of matrix B
  3. Select leading eigenvector (largest eigenvalue)
  4. Partition nodes based on eigenvector sign:
  5. Positive values → Community 1
  6. Negative values → Community 2

docs.title: Multi-Community Extension
docs.text:
For more than two communities:

  • Recursive bisection - Apply binary splitting repeatedly
  • Multiple eigenvectors - Use additional eigenvectors for finer partitioning
  • Eigenvalue significance - Only use eigenvectors with positive eigenvalues

docs.title: Negative Eigenvalues
docs.text:
Negative eigenvalues indicate: - Anti-communities - Fewer internal edges than expected - Bipartite structures - Natural separation patterns - Functional groupings - E.g., verbs vs nouns in text networks

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Zachary's Karate Club
docs.text:
The most famous validation of modularity clustering:

Background: Social network of 34 members of a karate club at a US university (1970)

Experiment: Club split due to internal dispute

Result: Modularity clustering predicted the exact split before it happened!

docs.title: Application Domains
docs.text: Domain Network Type Community Meaning Social Media User connections Interest groups, friend circles Biology Protein interactions Functional modules, pathways Neuroscience Brain connectivity Functional brain regions Technology Software dependencies Module clusters, subsystems Economics Trade networks Economic blocs, market segments Linguistics Word co-occurrence Semantic categories, grammar types

docs.title: Text Analysis Example
docs.text:
In word co-occurrence networks: - Circles (nouns) rarely connect to other circles - Squares (verbs) connect to both circles and squares - Modularity clustering naturally separates parts of speech

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Python Implementation
docs.text:
import numpy as np
import networkx as nx
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh

def modularity_clustering(adjacency_matrix):
    """
    Perform modularity clustering on a graph

    Parameters:
    adjacency_matrix: 2D numpy array representing graph adjacency

    Returns:
    communities: list of community assignments
    modularity_score: achieved modularity value
    """
    A = adjacency_matrix
    n = A.shape[0]
    m = np.sum(A) / 2  # Total edges

    # Calculate degree sequence
    degrees = np.sum(A, axis=1)

    # Construct modularity matrix
    B = A - np.outer(degrees, degrees) / (2 * m)

    # Find leading eigenvector
    eigenvals, eigenvecs = eigsh(B, k=1, which='LA')
    leading_eigenvec = eigenvecs[:, 0]

    # Partition based on eigenvector sign
    communities = (leading_eigenvec >= 0).astype(int)

    # Calculate modularity score
    modularity_score = calculate_modularity(A, communities)

    return communities, modularity_score

def calculate_modularity(A, communities):
    """Calculate modularity score for given partitioning"""
    n = A.shape[0]
    m = np.sum(A) / 2
    degrees = np.sum(A, axis=1)

    Q = 0
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            if communities[i] == communities[j]:
                Q += A[i, j] - (degrees[i] * degrees[j]) / (2 * m)

    return Q / (2 * m)

from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClusterMixin

class ModularityClustering(BaseEstimator, ClusterMixin):
    def __init__(self, resolution=1.0, random_state=None):
        self.resolution = resolution
        self.random_state = random_state

    def fit(self, X):
        # X is adjacency matrix or edge list
        self.labels_ = self._modularity_clustering(X)
        return self

    def fit_predict(self, X):
        return self.fit(X).labels_

docs.text: This case study analyzes air pollution data collected over 13 months, covering major pollutants and meteorological parameters in a city. The goal is to apply Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to reduce dimensionality while preserving critical patterns in the data.

📊 Duration: 13 months 📈 Frequency: Daily observations

docs.title: 3. Methodology
docs.text:

  2. Handle missing values (median for numerical columns, mode for categorical column 'Weather').

  3. Standardize features for PCA.

docs.title: 4. Python Implementation
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Load dataset
data = pd.read_csv('Air_Pollution.csv')

# Fill missing values
for col in data.columns:
    if col == "Weather":
        data[col].fillna(value=data[col].mode()[0], inplace=True)
    else:
        data[col].fillna(value=data[col].median(), inplace=True)

# Standardize data
scaler = StandardScaler()
data_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(data.select_dtypes(include=['float64', 'int64']))

# PCA
n = data_scaled.shape[1]
pca = PCA(n_components=n, random_state=1)
pca.fit(data_scaled)

# Explained variance
exp_var = pca.explained_variance_ratio_
print("Explained Variance Ratio:", exp_var)

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
When you think of sneakers for a trip, the importance of good footwear cannot be discarded, and the obvious brands that come to mind are Adidas and Nike. Adidas vs Nike is a constant debate as the two giants in the apparel market, with a large market cap and market share, battle it out to come on top.

As a newly hired Data Scientist in a market research company, you have been tasked with extracting insights from the data of men's and women's shoes and grouping products together to identify similarities and differences between the product range of these renowned brands.

🎯 Objective: Perform clustering on the products based on various factors to uncover patterns in pricing, discounts, and customer perception.

docs.title: 2. Dataset Description
docs.text:
The dataset contains 3,268 products from Nike and Adidas with the following attributes:

Column Name Description Product Name Name of the product Product ID Unique product identifier Listing Price Listed price of the product Sale Price Sale price of the product Discount Percentage discount offered Brand Brand name (Adidas/Nike) Rating Customer rating Reviews Number of reviews

📊 Source: Company-curated e-commerce dataset.

docs.title: 3. Methodology
docs.text:
1. Data Loading & Cleaning – Imported dataset, handled missing values, and ensured correct data types.
  2. Feature Selection – Selected numerical features relevant for clustering (price, discount, rating, reviews).
  3. Scaling – Standardized numerical columns to ensure equal weight in clustering.
  4. K-Means Clustering – Applied K-Means to group similar products.
  5. Evaluation – Used Elbow Method and Silhouette Score to determine optimal number of clusters.

docs.title: 4. Python Implementation
docs.text:
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Load dataset
df = pd.read_csv("data_air_nike.csv")

# Select relevant features
features = df[['Listing Price', 'Sale Price', 'Discount', 'Rating', 'Reviews']].dropna()

# Scaling
scaler = StandardScaler()
data_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(features)

# Determine WCSS for Elbow Method
WCSS = {}
for k in range(1, 10):
    kmeans = KMeans(n_clusters=k, random_state=1)
    kmeans.fit(data_scaled)
    WCSS[k] = kmeans.inertia_

# Plot Elbow Curve
plt.plot(list(WCSS.keys()), list(WCSS.values()), 'bx-')
plt.xlabel('Number of Clusters')
plt.ylabel('WCSS')
plt.title('Elbow Method')
plt.show()

👉 Open in Colab

docs.title: 5. Insights & Interpretation
docs.text:
• Optimal K was determined using the Elbow Method, suggesting K=3 clusters.
  • One cluster represented premium high-priced sneakers (avg. listing price ≈ $16,500).
  • Another cluster represented budget sneakers with high discounts (~45% average discount).
  • Mid-range sneakers formed the third cluster, balancing affordability and quality.

docs.text:

docs.title: Problem Context & Objectives
docs.text:
This tutorial demonstrates a comprehensive approach to predicting hospital length of stay (LOS) using machine learning techniques. The implementation addresses a critical healthcare management challenge: optimizing resource allocation through predictive analytics.

Business Problem: HealthPlus hospital faces revenue losses and operational inefficiencies due to poor resource allocation of beds, equipment, and staff. The solution involves developing a predictive model to estimate patient length of stay during admission.

Technical Objective: Build and validate a machine learning model that predicts LOS using patient admission data and initial test results, achieving interpretable results for clinical decision-making.

Dataset Scope: The analysis uses 500,000 patient admission records with 15 features including demographic data, admission details, health conditions, and hospital resource availability. The target variable is stay duration (3-51 days).

Practical Applications: The model enables hospitals to proactively plan treatment protocols, allocate staff efficiently, and optimize bed management, potentially reducing both costs and patient mortality through better resource distribution.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Structure Analysis
docs.text:
The implementation begins with comprehensive data exploration to understand the dataset's characteristics and identify potential modeling challenges.

Dataset Dimensions: 500,000 rows × 15 columns, representing a substantial sample size that provides statistical power for reliable model development. The large dataset size enables robust cross-validation and generalization testing.

Data Quality Assessment: Initial inspection reveals no missing values, which simplifies preprocessing but raises questions about data collection completeness. The absence of missing data in healthcare records is unusual and may indicate preprocessing or synthetic data generation.

Key Findings from Descriptive Statistics: - Target Variable Distribution: LOS ranges from 3-51 days with median of 9 days, showing right-skewed distribution typical in healthcare data - Resource Availability: Average 3 available rooms (0-24 range) and 5 available staff (0-10 range), indicating capacity constraints - Patient Demographics: 74% female patients, 75% aged 21-50, reflecting gynecology department dominance (68% of admissions)

Data Type Considerations: Mixed data types require careful encoding strategies. The presence of categorical variables like department names and doctor identifiers suggests that feature engineering will be crucial for model performance.

Limitations Identified: Patient ID analysis reveals repeat admissions (up to 21 times), but the notebook treats each admission independently, potentially missing temporal patterns or patient-specific factors that could improve predictions.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Univariate Analysis Implementation
docs.text:
The EDA phase employs custom visualization functions to systematically examine each variable's distribution characteristics and identify potential outliers or patterns.

Target Variable Analysis: The histogram-boxplot combination reveals that most patients stay 8-9 days, with few extending beyond 40 days. This distribution suggests that extreme cases are rare but may require specialized treatment protocols. The right-skewed nature indicates potential for log transformation in modeling.

Admission Deposit Patterns: Near-normal distribution with outliers suggests standardized pricing with exceptions for special cases. The range (\(1,654-\)7,000+) may correlate with treatment complexity and expected LOS.

Visitor Distribution Analysis: Highly right-skewed distribution with peaks at 2 and 4 visitors suggests cultural or policy factors affecting hospital visitation. This variable may serve as a proxy for illness severity or family support systems.

docs.title: Bivariate Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Correlation Assessment: The heatmap reveals no significant linear correlations between continuous variables, indicating that categorical variables likely drive LOS predictions. This finding justifies the focus on categorical feature analysis and suggests that simple linear relationships may be insufficient.

Ward-Based Analysis: - Ward A shows longest average LOS, confirmed to handle extreme cases and surgical patients - Wards B, D, F are gynecology-dedicated facilities with shorter stays - This specialization pattern supports department-specific resource planning

Age-Related Patterns: Patients aged 1-10 and 51-100 show longer stays, suggesting age-dependent care complexity. The U-shaped relationship indicates that both pediatric and geriatric care require extended hospitalization.

Clinical Significance: The bivariate analysis reveals that institutional factors (ward assignment, department) show stronger associations with LOS than patient characteristics, suggesting that hospital management practices significantly influence outcomes.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Categorical Encoding Strategy
docs.text:
The preprocessing phase implements one-hot encoding using pandas get_dummies with drop_first=True to avoid multicollinearity in regression modeling.

Encoding Rationale: One-hot encoding is chosen over label encoding because categorical variables (departments, doctors, wards) have no ordinal relationship. The drop_first parameter prevents perfect multicollinearity by creating k-1 dummy variables for k categories.

Feature Space Expansion: After encoding, the feature space expands significantly due to multiple categorical variables with many levels (9 doctors, 6 wards, 5 departments). This expansion increases model complexity but preserves all categorical information.

Train-Test Split Implementation: 80-20 split with random state ensures reproducibility. The large dataset size (400,000 training samples) provides sufficient data for reliable parameter estimation and reduces overfitting risk.

Preprocessing Limitations: The implementation doesn't address potential feature scaling for continuous variables or consider feature selection techniques to reduce dimensionality. Standard scaling might improve convergence in certain algorithms.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Statistical Modeling Approach
docs.text:
The implementation uses statsmodels OLS for comprehensive statistical analysis rather than sklearn's implementation, enabling detailed significance testing and assumption validation.

Model Performance Metrics: - R-squared: 0.84 indicates the model explains 84% of LOS variance - RMSE: ~2.7 days on test data represents typical prediction error - MAE: 2.15 days provides interpretable average prediction error - MAPE: ~19% shows relative prediction accuracy

Statistical Significance Analysis: Initial model reveals that Insurance, staff_available, and Visitors with Patient show p-values > 0.05, indicating insufficient predictive power at 95% confidence level. These variables are subsequently removed to improve model parsimony.

Coefficient Interpretation: - Department_surgery: +9.68 days vs. reference (TB&Chest_Disease), reflecting surgical complexity - Department_anesthesia: +6.08 days, indicating severe cases requiring specialized care - Doctor_Dr Simon: +6.14 days vs. reference (Dr Isaac), suggesting surgical specialist handling complex cases

Model Validation: Train-test performance similarity (RMSE: 2.67 train vs. 2.70 test) indicates good generalization without overfitting, validating the model's reliability for production use.

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Comprehensive Assumption Validation
docs.text:
The implementation systematically tests linear regression assumptions to ensure statistical validity and reliable inference.

Multicollinearity Assessment: VIF analysis shows all continuous variables have VIF < 5, confirming no problematic multicollinearity. However, the note about dummy variables having naturally high VIF values highlights a common statistical misconception that the implementation correctly addresses.

Residual Analysis Results: - Mean of residuals: ~0 (satisfied) - Normality: Histogram and distribution plots confirm approximately normal residuals - Linearity: Residuals vs. fitted values show random scatter without systematic patterns - Homoscedasticity: Goldfeld-Quandt test (p > 0.05) confirms constant variance assumption

Statistical Test Interpretation: The Goldfeld-Quandt test specifically tests for heteroscedasticity by comparing variances in different data segments. The non-significant result (p > 0.05) supports the homoscedasticity assumption, validating standard error calculations.

Diagnostic Limitations: While formal tests pass, the implementation could benefit from additional diagnostics like Cook's distance for outlier detection and leverage analysis for influential observations.

↩ Back to Top

# Function to plot a boxplot and a histogram along the same scale
def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Boxplot and histogram combined

    data: dataframe
    feature: dataframe column
    figsize: size of figure (default (12,7))
    kde: whether to the show density curve (default False)
    bins: number of bins for histogram (default None)
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows = 2,      # Number of rows of the subplot grid = 2
        sharex = True,  # x-axis will be shared among all subplots
        gridspec_kw = {"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)},
        figsize = figsize,
    )                   # Creating the 2 subplots
    sns.boxplot(data = data, x = feature, ax = ax_box2, showmeans = True, color = "violet"
    )                   # Boxplot will be created and a star will indicate the mean value of the column
    sns.histplot(
        data = data, x = feature, kde = kde, ax = ax_hist2, bins = bins, palette = "winter"
    ) if bins else sns.histplot(
        data = data, x = feature, kde = kde, ax = ax_hist2
    )                   # For histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].mean(), color = "green", linestyle = "--"
    )                   # Add mean to the histogram
    ax_hist2.axvline(
        data[feature].median(), color = "black", linestyle = "-"
    )                   # Add median to the histogram

docs.title: Performance Metrics Implementation
docs.text:
# Function to compute adjusted R-squared
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]
    k = predictors.shape[1]
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))

# Function to compute MAPE
def mape_score(targets, predictions):
    return np.mean(np.abs(targets - predictions) / targets) * 100

# Function to compute different metrics to check performance of a regression model
def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check regression model performance

    model: regressor
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    pred = model.predict(predictors)                  # Predict using the independent variables
    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)                       # To compute R-squared
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)    # To compute adjusted R-squared
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))  # To compute RMSE
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)           # To compute MAE
    mape = mape_score(target, pred)                   # To compute MAPE

    # Creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "RMSE": rmse,
            "MAE": mae,
            "R-squared": r2,
            "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
            "MAPE": mape,
        },
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

Mathematical Foundations: - Adjusted R²: 1 - ((1-R²)(n-1)/(n-k-1)) - penalizes model complexity - MAPE: Provides percentage-based error interpretation for business decisions - Comprehensive Framework: Enables consistent model comparison across algorithms

docs.title: Multicollinearity Diagnostics
docs.text:
from statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence import variance_inflation_factor

def checking_vif(train):
    vif = pd.DataFrame()
    vif["feature"] = train.columns

    # Calculating VIF for each feature
    vif["VIF"] = [
        variance_inflation_factor(train.values, i) for i in range(len(train.columns))
    ]
    return vif

print(checking_vif(x_train1))

VIF Interpretation: - Formula: VIF = 1/(1-R²) where R² comes from regressing each predictor against others - VIF < 5 for all continuous variables → No multicollinearity problems - Dummy variables naturally have higher VIF due to categorical structure

docs.text:

residual.mean()
Result: ≈ 0, confirming unbiased predictions.

Assumption 2: Normality of Error Terms

Histogram shows approximately normal distribution - assumption satisfied.

Assumption 3: Linearity 

# Predicted values
fitted = olsmodel2.fittedvalues

# Plotting Residuals VS Fitted Values
sns.residplot(x = fitted, y = residual, color="lightblue")
plt.xlabel("Fitted Values")
plt.ylabel("Residual")
plt.title("Residual PLOT")
plt.show()
Random scatter pattern confirms linearity assumption.

Assumption 4: Homoscedasticity 

import statsmodels.stats.api as sms
from statsmodels.compat import lzip

name = ["F statistic", "p-value"]
test = sms.het_goldfeldquandt(residual, x_train2)
lzip(name, test)

Goldfeld-Quandt Test: - H₀: Homoscedastic residuals - H₁: Heteroscedastic residuals - Result: p > 0.05 → Fail to reject H₀ → Homoscedasticity confirmed

docs.title: Project Context and Objectives
docs.text: Healthcare resource allocation represents a critical challenge amplified during the COVID-19 pandemic. This tutorial addresses a fundamental problem: predicting patient length of stay (LOS) to optimize hospital resource management. The HealthPlus hospital scenario provides a realistic framework for understanding how predictive modeling can directly impact operational efficiency and patient outcomes.

docs.title: Business Problem Definition
docs.text:
HealthPlus hospital faces significant revenue losses and suboptimal patient outcomes due to inefficient resource allocation. The core challenge involves predicting patient LOS during admission to enable:

  • Proactive resource planning for beds, equipment, and staff
  • Improved patient flow management throughout the hospital system
  • Cost optimization through better capacity utilization
  • Enhanced care quality via appropriate resource allocation

docs.title: Methodological Approach
docs.text:
This analysis employs a systematic regression modeling approach:

  1. Comprehensive data exploration to understand patient demographics and admission patterns
  2. Statistical correlation analysis to identify key predictive relationships
  3. Multiple regression techniques including regularization methods
  4. Feature selection optimization to balance model complexity and performance
  5. Critical performance evaluation across multiple metrics

The tutorial demonstrates how statistical modeling translates into actionable healthcare insights while maintaining analytical rigor.

docs.title: Dataset Characteristics
docs.text:
The healthcare dataset contains 500,000 patient records with 15 features capturing admission-time information. This substantial sample size enables robust statistical inference while presenting computational considerations for model training.

Key Dataset Properties: - Scale: 500,000 patients × 15 features - Completeness: No missing values detected - Scope: Admitted patients only (excludes outpatient visits) - Temporal Range: Cross-sectional admission data

docs.text:

Admission Context: - Admission type (trauma, emergency, urgent) - Severity classification (extreme, moderate, minor) - Insurance status and deposit amounts

Hospital Infrastructure: - Available rooms and staff capacity - Department and ward assignments - Attending physician information

docs.title: Data Quality Assessment
docs.text:
The analysis reveals several important characteristics:

Strengths: - Complete data with no missing values - Large sample size supporting statistical power - Comprehensive feature set covering clinical and operational factors

Limitations: - Patient ID shows multiple admissions (up to 21 per patient), potentially introducing dependency - Cross-sectional design limits causal inference - No temporal tracking of patient progression during stay

Critical Insight: The maximum 21 admissions per patient suggests either chronic conditions requiring frequent hospitalization or data collection spanning multiple years. This repeat patient pattern requires careful consideration in model validation to avoid data leakage.

docs.title: Correlation Analysis Results
docs.text:
A critical finding emerges from correlation analysis: continuous variables show minimal correlation with LOS, suggesting categorical variables drive prediction accuracy. This insight fundamentally shapes the modeling approach, emphasizing the importance of categorical feature engineering over numerical transformation.

Key Correlations: - Continuous variables: Near-zero correlation with LOS - Categorical relationships: Stronger associations observed - Feature independence: Minimal multicollinearity among predictors

This ward-based segmentation suggests resource allocation varies significantly by patient severity, with specialized wards requiring different staffing and equipment strategies.

docs.title: Age-Related LOS Patterns
docs.text:
Notable finding: Patients aged 1-10 and 51-100 years exhibit longer stays, contrasting with the 21-50 demographic. def histogram_boxplot(data, feature, figsize=(12, 7), kde=False, bins=None):
    """
    Combined boxplot and histogram visualization

    Parameters:
    -----------
    data : DataFrame
        Source dataframe
    feature : str
        Column name to visualize
    figsize : tuple
        Figure dimensions (width, height)
    kde : bool
        Whether to overlay kernel density estimation
    bins : int or None
        Number of histogram bins
    """
    f2, (ax_box2, ax_hist2) = plt.subplots(
        nrows=2,                                    # Two-panel layout
        sharex=True,                               # Shared x-axis for alignment
        gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": (0.25, 0.75)}, # Box plot smaller than histogram
        figsize=figsize,
    )

    # Boxplot with mean indicator
    sns.boxplot(
        data=data, 
        x=feature, 
        ax=ax_box2, 
        showmeans=True,      # Star marker for mean
        color="violet"
    )

    # Histogram with optional KDE
    if bins:
        sns.histplot(data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2, bins=bins, palette="winter")
    else:
        sns.histplot(data=data, x=feature, kde=kde, ax=ax_hist2)

    # Statistical reference lines
    ax_hist2.axvline(data[feature].mean(), color="green", linestyle="--")    # Mean
    ax_hist2.axvline(data[feature].median(), color="black", linestyle="-")   # Median

Function Design Rationale: - Dual visualization: Boxplot reveals outliers while histogram shows distribution shape - Statistical references: Mean and median lines provide central tendency context - Flexible parameters: Adaptable to different variable types and analysis needs

def stacked_barplot(data, predictor, target):
    """
    Create stacked bar plots for categorical relationships

    Parameters:
    -----------
    data : DataFrame
        Source dataframe
    predictor : str
        Independent categorical variable
    target : str
        Target categorical variable for stacking
    """
    count = data[predictor].nunique()
    sorter = data[target].value_counts().index[-1]

    # Absolute counts crosstab
    tab1 = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], margins=True).sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )
    print(tab1)
    print("-" * 120)

    # Proportional crosstab
    tab = pd.crosstab(data[predictor], data[target], normalize="index").sort_values(
        by=sorter, ascending=False
    )

docs.title: Performance Metrics Framework
docs.text:
def adj_r2_score(predictors, targets, predictions):
    """
    Calculate adjusted R-squared for regression models

    Formula: 1 - ((1 - R²) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))
    where n = sample size, k = number of predictors
    """
    r2 = r2_score(targets, predictions)
    n = predictors.shape[0]  # Number of observations
    k = predictors.shape[1]  # Number of predictors
    return 1 - ((1 - r2) * (n - 1) / (n - k - 1))

def mape_score(targets, predictions):
    """
    Mean Absolute Percentage Error calculation

    Formula: mean(|actual - predicted| / |actual|) * 100
    """
    return np.mean(np.abs(targets - predictions) / targets) * 100

def model_performance_regression(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Comprehensive regression model evaluation

    Returns:
    --------
    DataFrame with RMSE, MAE, R-squared, Adjusted R-squared, MAPE
    """
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    # Core metrics calculation
    r2 = r2_score(target, pred)
    adjr2 = adj_r2_score(predictors, target, pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(target, pred))
    mae = mean_absolute_error(target, pred)
    mape = mape_score(target, pred)

    # Results dataframe
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame({
        "RMSE": rmse,
        "MAE": mae,
        "R-squared": r2,
        "Adj. R-squared": adjr2,
        "MAPE": mape,
    }, index=[0])

    return df_perf

Metric Implementation Details: - Adjusted R²: Penalizes model complexity, essential for feature selection - RMSE vs MAE: RMSE penalizes large errors more heavily than MAE - MAPE: Provides interpretable percentage error for business stakeholders - DataFrame output: Consistent format for model comparison

docs.title: Statistical Significance Testing
docs.text:
from scipy import stats

def prediction_confidence_interval(model, X, alpha=0.05):
    """
    Calculate prediction confidence intervals for linear regression

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : sklearn LinearRegression
        Fitted linear regression model
    X : array-like
        Feature matrix for predictions
    alpha : float
        Significance level (default 0.05 for 95% CI)

    Returns:
    --------
    tuple : (predictions, lower_bound, upper_bound)
    """
    predictions = model.predict(X)

    # Calculate residual standard error
    residuals = y_train - model.predict(x_train)
    mse = np.mean(residuals ** 2)
    se = np.sqrt(mse)

    # t-statistic for confidence interval
    t_val = stats.t.ppf(1 - alpha/2, df=len(y_train) - X.shape[1] - 1)

    # Standard error of prediction
    se_pred = se * np.sqrt(1 + np.diag(X @ np.linalg.inv(x_train.T @ x_train) @ X.T))

    # Confidence intervals
    lower_bound = predictions - t_val * se_pred
    upper_bound = predictions + t_val * se_pred

    return predictions, lower_bound, upper_bound

def robust_model_evaluation(model, X, y, cv_folds=10, random_state=42):
    """
    Comprehensive cross-validation evaluation

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : sklearn estimator
        Model to evaluate
    X : array-like
        Feature matrix
    y : array-like
        Target vector
    cv_folds : int
        Number of cross-validation folds
    random_state : int
        Random state for reproducibility

    Returns:
    --------
    dict : Cross-validation results
    """
    # Cross-validation setup
    cv = KFold(n_splits=cv_folds, shuffle=True, random_state=random_state)

    # Multiple scoring metrics
    scoring_metrics = ['r2', 'neg_mean_squared_error', 'neg_mean_absolute_error']

    cv_results = {}
    for metric in scoring_metrics:
        scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring=metric)
        cv_results[metric] = {
            'mean': scores.mean(),
            'std': scores.std(),
            'scores': scores
        }

    return cv_results

# Example usage

docs.title: Residual Analysis Implementation
docs.text:
def residual_analysis(model, X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test):
    """
    Comprehensive residual analysis for regression diagnostics

    Parameters:
    -----------
    model : fitted sklearn model
    X_train, y_train : training data
    X_test, y_test : testing data

    Returns:
    --------
    dict : Residual analysis results
    """
    # Generate predictions
    train_pred = model.predict(X_train)
    test_pred = model.predict(X_test)

    # Calculate residuals
    train_residuals = y_train - train_pred
    test_residuals = y_test - test_pred

    # Residual analysis
    analysis = {
        'train_residual_mean': train_residuals.mean(),
        'test_residual_mean': test_residuals.mean(),
        'train_residual_std': train_residuals.std(),
        'test_residual_std': test_residuals.std(),
        'train_residuals': train_residuals,
        'test_residuals': test_residuals,
    }

    # Visualization
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(15, 10))

    # Residuals vs fitted
    axes[0, 0].scatter(train_pred, train_residuals, alpha=0.5)
    axes[0, 0].axhline(y=0, color='red', linestyle='--')
    axes[0, 0].set_title('Residuals vs Fitted (Training)')
    axes[0, 0].set_xlabel('Fitted Values')
    axes[0, 0].set_ylabel('Residuals')

    # QQ plot for normality
    stats.probplot(train_residuals, dist="norm", plot=axes[0, 1])
    axes[0, 1].set_title('Normal Q-Q Plot (Training Residuals)')

    # Histogram of residuals
    axes[1, 0].hist(train_residuals, bins=50, alpha=0.7)
    axes[1, 0].set_title('Distribution of Training Residuals')
    axes[1, 0].set_xlabel('Residuals')
    axes[1, 0].set_ylabel('Frequency')

    # Residuals vs predicted (test set)
    axes[1, 1].scatter(test_pred, test_residuals, alpha=0.5, color='orange')
    axes[1, 1].axhline(y=0, color='red', linestyle='--')
    axes[1, 1].set_title('Residuals vs Fitted (Testing)')
    axes[1, 1].set_xlabel('Fitted Values')
    axes[1, 1].set_ylabel('Residuals')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    return analysis

# Example usage
residual_results = residual_analysis(model, x_train, y_train, x_test, y_test)

def create_production_pipeline(selected_features, model_params=None):
    """
    Create production-ready prediction pipeline

    Parameters:
    -----------
    selected_features : list
        Feature names selected through feature selection
    model_params : dict
        Model hyperparameters if needed

    Returns:
    --------
    Pipeline object ready for deployment
    """
    from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
    from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
    from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

    # Feature selection transformer
    feature_selector = ColumnTransformer([
        ('selected', 'passthrough', selected_features)
    ], remainder='drop')

    # Model pipeline
    if model_params is None:
        model_params = {}

    pipeline = Pipeline([
        ('feature_selection', feature_selector),
        ('regressor', LinearRegression(**model_params))
    ])

    return pipeline

# Example pipeline creation

    selected_features=list(x_train.columns[feat_cols])
)

# Fit and validate pipeline

pipeline_predictions = production_pipeline.predict(x_test)

The 8-feature model represents the optimal balance between predictive accuracy and operational simplicity, making it the recommended approach for clinical deployment. docs.title: Problem Statement
docs.text: BigMart, a major retail chain, faces the critical challenge of predicting sales performance across its 10 stores spanning different cities. With 1559 products generating 2013 sales data, the organization needs to understand which product and store characteristics drive revenue growth.

docs.title: Strategic Importance
docs.text:
This predictive analytics project addresses three core business needs:

  1. Inventory Management: Optimize stock levels based on predicted demand patterns
  2. Store Performance: Identify factors that differentiate high-performing from underperforming outlets
  3. Product Strategy: Understand which product characteristics correlate with higher sales

docs.title: Methodology Overview
docs.text:
Our approach employs linear regression modeling with comprehensive preprocessing, feature engineering, and statistical validation. This methodology provides both predictive capability and interpretable insights for business decision-making.

Key Analytical Framework: - Univariate Analysis: Understanding individual variable distributions - Bivariate Analysis: Exploring relationships between predictors and sales - Missing Value Treatment: Pattern-based imputation strategies - Feature Engineering: Creating meaningful derived variables - Model Building: Iterative regression with assumption validation - Statistical Testing: VIF analysis and hypothesis testing for feature selection

docs.title: Expected Outcomes
docs.text:
The final model will deliver: - Quantitative Predictions: Sales forecasts for test dataset products - Interpretable Coefficients: Understanding of factor impacts on sales - Actionable Recommendations: Data-driven strategies for sales improvement

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Structure Analysis
docs.text:
The BigMart dataset contains 8,523 training observations and 5,681 test observations with 11 feature variables and 1 target variable.

Variable Categories: - Categorical Variables (5): Item_Fat_Content, Item_Type, Outlet_Size, Outlet_Location_Type, Outlet_Type - Numerical Variables (5): Item_Weight, Item_Visibility, Item_MRP, Outlet_Establishment_Year, Item_Outlet_Sales (target) - Identifier Variables (2): Item_Identifier, Outlet_Identifier (removed for modeling)

docs.title: Critical Data Quality Issues Identified
docs.text:
1. Inconsistent Categorical Encoding The Item_Fat_Content variable shows inconsistent labeling: - "Low Fat" appears as "low fat", "LF", and "Low Fat" - "Regular" appears as "reg" and "Regular"

Business Impact: This inconsistency would create artificial categories, diluting the statistical power of the fat content variable in predicting sales.

2. Missing Value Patterns - Item_Weight: 17% missing values - Outlet_Size: 28% missing values

Strategic Implication: The high percentage of missing values requires careful treatment to avoid introducing bias into sales predictions.

docs.title: Data Preprocessing Strategy
docs.text:
Categorical Standardization: Applied lambda functions to normalize Item_Fat_Content categories, ensuring consistent encoding across training and test datasets.

Identifier Removal: Eliminated Item_Identifier and Outlet_Identifier as these provide no predictive value for sales forecasting.

Missing Value Preparation: Conducted exploratory analysis to identify patterns that would inform imputation strategies rather than arbitrary mean/median replacement.

docs.title: Quality Assurance Validation
docs.text:
Post-preprocessing validation confirmed: - Consistent categorical encodings across all variables - No remaining identifier variables - Preserved data distribution characteristics - Equivalent transformations applied to both training and test datasets

Limitations: The preprocessing approach assumes that inconsistent labeling was purely data entry error rather than meaningful business distinctions. Additionally, the removal of identifier variables assumes no geographic or product-specific effects that transcend measured characteristics.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Univariate Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Categorical Variable Distributions:

The analysis revealed several important business patterns:

Item_Fat_Content Distribution: After standardization, Low Fat products significantly outnumber Regular products, suggesting either consumer preference trends or strategic product mix decisions.

Outlet_Size Hierarchy: Medium-sized outlets dominate (after imputation), followed by Small and High outlets. This distribution pattern suggests a strategic focus on medium-format retail.

Geographic Distribution: Tier 3 locations represent the largest segment, followed by Tier 2 and Tier 1. This indicates BigMart's focus on smaller cities and towns rather than metropolitan areas.

Store Format Analysis: Supermarket Type 1 dominates the outlet mix, with roughly equal representation across Types 2, 3, and Grocery Stores.

Product Category Leadership: Fruits and Vegetables constitute the largest product category, followed by Snack Foods and Household items, reflecting typical grocery shopping patterns.

docs.title: Numerical Variable Characteristics
docs.text:
Item_Weight: Exhibits approximately uniform distribution, which simplified missing value treatment strategies.

Item_Visibility: Shows right-skewed distribution, indicating some products receive disproportionately high display allocation.

Item_MRP: Demonstrates multi-modal distribution, suggesting distinct pricing tiers in BigMart's product strategy.

docs.title: Bivariate Analysis Findings
docs.text:
Temporal Sales Patterns: Analysis of Outlet_Establishment_Year vs. Item_Outlet_Sales revealed relatively constant average sales across years, with a notable sales drop in 1998. This pattern suggests: - Store age may not be a primary sales driver - External economic factors (possibly economic crisis) impacted 1998 performance - Consistent operational standards across different store vintages

Correlation Analysis Results: - Item_MRP: Moderate positive correlation with sales (strongest predictor identified) - Item_Weight: No significant correlation with sales - Item_Visibility: Weak negative correlation, suggesting potential inverse relationship

docs.title: Critical Business Insights
docs.text:
1. Price-Sales Relationship: The strong correlation between Item_MRP and sales indicates that higher-priced items generate more revenue, supporting premium product strategies.

2. Visibility Paradox: The inverse relationship between visibility and sales suggests management may be allocating premium display space to slower-moving products to boost their performance.

3. Store Format Implications: The dominance of Supermarket Type 1 in the data may indicate this format's success or simply reflect corporate expansion strategy.

docs.title: Analytical Limitations
docs.text:
• Temporal Scope: Single-year data (2013) limits ability to identify seasonal patterns or long-term trends
  • Causality Questions: Correlation analysis cannot establish whether high MRP causes high sales or reflects demand-driven pricing
  • External Factors: The 1998 sales anomaly suggests unmeasured external variables impact performance

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Pattern-Based Imputation Approach
docs.text: Rather than applying simple mean/median imputation, the analysis employed relationship-based imputation that preserves data integrity and business logic.

docs.title: Item_Weight Imputation Analysis
docs.text:
Cross-Variable Pattern Investigation: The analysis examined Item_Weight relationships across multiple categorical combinations:

Finding 1: Item_Fat_Content × Item_Type combinations showed average weights ranging from 10-14 units, with relatively consistent patterns across categories.

Finding 2: Outlet_Type × Outlet_Location_Type combinations demonstrated consistent average weights around 13 units.

Finding 3: Item_Fat_Content × Outlet_Size combinations also showed stable weight averages around 13 units.

Imputation Strategy: Based on the consistent 10-14 range across all categorical combinations, missing Item_Weight values were imputed using a uniform distribution with parameters a=10, b=14.

Rationale: This approach maintains the original uniform distribution while incorporating business logic that weight ranges should remain consistent across product categories.

docs.title: Outlet_Size Imputation Analysis
docs.text:
Pattern Recognition Process:

Step 1: Analysis of missing Outlet_Size patterns revealed that most missing values occurred in: - Supermarket Type 1 outlets - Tier 2 locations - Low Fat product categories

Step 2: Cross-tabulation analysis identified deterministic patterns: - All Grocery Stores: Small outlet size - All Supermarket Type 2 & 3: Medium outlet size - All Tier 2 locations: Small outlet size

Implementation Strategy: Applied rule-based imputation: - Grocery Store outlets → Small - Tier 2 locations → Small

docs.title: Imputation Validation
docs.text:
Distribution Preservation: Post-imputation analysis confirmed that: - Item_Weight maintained its uniform distribution characteristics - Outlet_Size distribution aligned with business logic expectations - No artificial bias was introduced into the target variable relationship

Business Logic Consistency: The imputation rules reflected logical business relationships: - Grocery stores are typically smaller format - Tier 2 cities typically house smaller stores - Weight consistency across product categories makes operational sense

docs.title: Strategic Implications
docs.text:
Inventory Management: The weight imputation strategy ensures that demand forecasting models won't be biased by missing weight data, supporting accurate inventory calculations.

Store Classification: The outlet size imputation enables proper store format analysis, crucial for understanding performance differences across store types.

docs.title: Methodological Limitations
docs.text:
Assumption Risk: The approach assumes that missing data patterns reflect the same relationships as observed data, which may not hold if missing values are systematically different.

Temporal Stability: The patterns observed in 2013 data may not persist across different time periods or market conditions.

External Validation: The imputation strategy lacks validation against external data sources or business records.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Feature Engineering Strategy
docs.text:
Outlet_Age Creation: Generated a new variable calculating store age as (2013 - Outlet_Establishment_Year), based on the hypothesis that older stores might have higher sales due to established customer relationships.

Hypothesis Testing Result: Subsequent analysis revealed that store age showed minimal relationship with sales performance, contradicting the initial business hypothesis. This finding suggests that: - Store operational quality matters more than tenure - Market saturation may offset experience advantages - BigMart's operational standards maintain consistency across store ages

docs.title: Systematic Feature Selection Process
docs.text: The modeling process employed a rigorous iterative feature elimination approach using statistical significance testing and multicollinearity analysis.

docs.title: Multicollinearity Assessment
docs.text:
Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Analysis:

Initial Assessment: Outlet_Age showed high VIF scores (>5), indicating problematic collinearity with other temporal variables.

Decision Logic: Variables with VIF > 5 were systematically removed to prevent unstable coefficient estimates.

Business Interpretation: High multicollinearity would make it impossible to isolate individual variable effects, compromising the model's interpretability for business decision-making.

docs.title: Statistical Significance Testing
docs.text:
P-Value Analysis Framework:

Applied hypothesis testing for each variable: - Null Hypothesis: Variable has no relationship with sales - Alternative Hypothesis: Variable significantly predicts sales - Significance Threshold: p < 0.05

Elimination Sequence: 1. Item_Type categories: All p-values > 0.05 (collectively removed) 2. Item_Weight: p-value = 0.724 (removed) 3. Outlet_Location_Type: Both categories p > 0.05 (removed) 4. Outlet_Size: Both categories p > 0.05 (removed) 5. Item_Visibility: p-value = 0.064 (removed)

docs.title: Final Feature Set
docs.text: Retained Variables: - Item_MRP: Strong predictor (coefficient = 1.9555) - Item_Fat_Content_Regular: Significant category effect (coefficient = 0.0158) - Outlet_Type categories: All three supermarket types significant predictors

docs.title: Feature Selection Implications
docs.text:
Model Parsimony: The final model includes only 5 variables from the original 10+ feature set, achieving strong predictive power (R² = 0.720) with minimal complexity.

Business Interpretability: The reduced feature set focuses on actionable variables: - Pricing Strategy (Item_MRP) - Product Mix (Fat Content) - Store Format (Outlet Type)

Operational Focus: The elimination of variables like Item_Weight, Visibility, and Location Type suggests these factors are either: - Not directly controllable for sales improvement - Already optimized across the BigMart network - Secondary to format and pricing strategies

docs.title: Critical Assessment
docs.text:
Selection Bias Risk: The stepwise elimination process may have removed variables that, while individually non-significant, could contribute meaningfully in combination.

Business Logic vs. Statistical Significance: Some eliminated variables (like Item_Visibility) may have practical business importance despite statistical non-significance in this dataset.

Temporal Limitations: The feature selection is based on 2013 data patterns, which may not reflect current market dynamics or consumer preferences.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 5]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Model Development Process
docs.text: The linear regression development followed a systematic assumption-driven approach, ensuring statistical validity before drawing business conclusions.

docs.title: Initial Model Performance
docs.text:
Starting Point: The initial model with all scaled features achieved R² = 0.563, indicating moderate explanatory power but significant room for improvement.

Feature Engineering Impact: After systematic feature selection, the model maintained similar R² (~0.56) with significantly fewer variables, demonstrating that removed features added minimal predictive value.

docs.title: Assumption Validation and Model Refinement
docs.text:
1. Residual Mean Assessment - Requirement: Mean of residuals ≈ 0 - Result: Achieved (residual mean ≈ 0) - Interpretation: No systematic bias in model predictions

2. Normality of Error Terms - Test Method: Histogram analysis and visual inspection - Result: Residuals approximately normally distributed - Business Implication: Confidence intervals and significance tests are reliable

3. Linearity Assessment - Initial Evaluation: Residual vs. fitted values plot showed clear pattern - Problem Identified: Non-linear relationship between predictors and target - Solution Applied: Log transformation of target variable

docs.title: Transformation Impact Analysis
docs.text:
Log Transformation Results: - R² Improvement: 0.563 → 0.720 (significant enhancement) - Linearity Achievement: Residual plots showed random distribution post-transformation - Model Interpretation: Changed from predicting raw sales to predicting log(sales)

Business Translation: The log transformation means: - Coefficients represent proportional rather than absolute changes - Model captures multiplicative rather than additive effects - More appropriate for sales data which typically shows exponential patterns

docs.title: Final Model Equation
docs.text:
Mathematical Formula: 

log(Item_Outlet_Sales) = 4.6356 + 1.9555 × Item_MRP + 0.0158 × Item_Fat_Content_Regular + 1.9550 × Outlet_Type_Supermarket_Type1 + 1.7737 × Outlet_Type_Supermarket_Type2 + 2.4837 × Outlet_Type_Supermarket_Type3

docs.title: Coefficient Interpretation
docs.text:
Item_MRP (1.9555): A one-unit increase in (scaled) MRP increases log(sales) by 1.9555 units. This represents the strongest individual predictor.

Item_Fat_Content_Regular (0.0158): Regular fat products have slightly higher log(sales) than Low Fat products (reference category).

Outlet_Type Coefficients: - Supermarket Type 3 (2.4837): Highest sales performance - Supermarket Type 1 (1.9550): Moderate performance - Supermarket Type 2 (1.7737): Lower performance - Grocery Store: Reference category (lowest performance)

docs.title: Model Performance Metrics
docs.text: Training Performance: - R-squared: 0.720 (explains 72% of sales variance) - Adjusted R-squared: High value indicates good fit accounting for variables - MSE: 0.288 (on log scale) - RMSE: 0.537 (on log scale)

docs.title: Cross-Validation Results
docs.text: 10-Fold Cross-Validation: - Mean R²: 0.718 (consistent with training) - Mean MSE: 0.290 (stable performance) - Performance Assessment: Model shows good generalization (just right fit)

docs.title: Business Strategy Implications
docs.text:
Pricing Strategy: The strong MRP coefficient suggests revenue optimization through strategic pricing rather than volume-focused discounting.

Store Format Strategy: Supermarket Type 3 format shows superior performance, suggesting expansion or conversion opportunities.

Product Mix Optimization: The minimal fat content effect suggests this is not a primary driver for sales optimization.

docs.title: Model Limitations
docs.text:
Linearity Assumption: Even after log transformation, linear regression assumes constant proportional relationships, which may not hold across all price ranges or store formats.

Feature Interactions: The model doesn't capture potential interaction effects between MRP and store format or other variable combinations.

Temporal Stability: Coefficients based on 2013 data may not reflect current market dynamics or consumer preferences.

External Factors: The model cannot account for competition, local economic conditions, or seasonal variations not captured in the dataset.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 6]

docs.title: Comprehensive Assumption Testing
docs.text: Linear regression requires four critical assumptions to be valid. The analysis systematically tested and addressed each assumption.

docs.title: Mean of Residuals Validation
docs.text: Test Result: Residual mean = -1.48e-15 (essentially 0) Status: ✅ Assumption satisfied Interpretation: The model shows no systematic bias in predictions, indicating unbiased coefficient estimates.

docs.title: Normality of Error Terms
docs.text: Visual Assessment: Histogram of residuals with KDE overlay showed approximately normal distribution Statistical Implication: Confidence intervals and hypothesis tests are statistically reliable Business Impact: Prediction intervals for sales forecasts will be accurate

docs.title: Linearity Testing and Resolution
docs.text:
Initial Problem: Residual vs. fitted values plot revealed systematic patterns, indicating non-linear relationships

Pattern Analysis: The funnel-shaped residual pattern suggested heteroscedasticity and potential non-linearity

Solution Implementation: Applied log transformation to the target variable (Item_Outlet_Sales)

Validation Result: Post-transformation residual plots showed random scatter, confirming linearity assumption satisfaction

Performance Impact: Model R² improved from 0.563 to 0.720, representing a substantial improvement in explanatory power

docs.title: Homoscedasticity Testing
docs.text: Test Applied: Goldfeld-Quandt test for heteroscedasticity Null Hypothesis: Residuals are homoscedastic (constant variance) Test Result: p-value > 0.05 Conclusion: Failed to reject null hypothesis - residuals are homoscedastic Statistical Validation: ✅ Assumption satisfied

docs.title: Transformation Interpretation Impact
docs.text:
Model Output Change: The log transformation fundamentally changed the model's interpretation:

Original Scale: Predicting absolute sales values Log Scale: Predicting proportional changes in sales

Business Translation: - Coefficients now represent percentage impacts rather than absolute dollar impacts - More appropriate for sales data which typically exhibits multiplicative rather than additive relationships - Better captures the reality that sales impacts are often proportional to current sales levels

docs.title: Cross-Validation Robustness
docs.text:
10-Fold Cross-Validation Results: - Training R²: 0.720 - CV Mean R²: 0.718 ± 0.040 - Training MSE: 0.288 - CV Mean MSE: 0.290 ± 0.058

Overfitting Assessment: The minimal difference between training and cross-validation performance indicates the model generalizes well and is not overfitted.

Model Stability: Low standard deviations in CV metrics suggest consistent performance across different data subsets.

docs.title: Residual Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Homogeneity Validation: The random scatter in final residual plots confirms that the model appropriately captures the underlying relationship without systematic patterns.

Outlier Assessment: No extreme outliers were identified that would compromise model reliability.

Prediction Reliability: The satisfied assumptions ensure that confidence intervals for individual predictions and coefficients are statistically valid.

docs.title: Assumption Testing Limitations
docs.text:
Sample Size Considerations: While the 8,523 observations provide adequate power for assumption testing, some tests may be sensitive to the large sample size.

Transformation Trade-offs: The log transformation improved linearity but requires back-transformation for business interpretation, introducing potential prediction bias.

Assumption Interdependence: Some assumption violations can mask others; the sequential testing approach may not capture all interaction effects.

docs.title: Business Validation Implications
docs.text:
Prediction Reliability: With all assumptions satisfied, the model's sales predictions can be trusted for business planning and inventory management.

Coefficient Interpretation: The statistically valid coefficients provide reliable guidance for pricing strategies and store format decisions.

Performance Monitoring: The assumption validation framework can be reapplied as new data becomes available to ensure continued model validity.
