docs.title: The Challenge
docs.text: McCurr Health Consultancy faces a critical HR challenge that many multinational corporations encounter: high employee attrition costs. The company currently invests heavily in retention initiatives across all employees, but the Head of People Operations seeks a more targeted, cost-effective approach.

docs.title: Strategic Objective
docs.text: Transform from blanket retention spending to predictive, targeted retention by identifying employees at highest risk of attrition before they leave.

docs.title: Expected Business Impact
docs.text:
• Cost Reduction: Focus retention incentives only on at-risk employees

  • Talent Retention: Prevent loss of valuable employees through early intervention

  • Resource Optimization: Allocate HR resources more strategically

  • Competitive Advantage: Maintain workforce stability in competitive markets

docs.title: Success Metrics
docs.text:
The project's success will be measured by the model's ability to correctly identify employees who will leave (high recall for attrition class), minimizing false negatives that result in losing valuable talent.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1: Environment Setup & Data Loading]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Characteristics
docs.text:
The dataset contains 2,940 employee records with 34 variables covering three key areas:

  • Demographic Information: Age, gender, marital status, education
  • Work-Related Metrics: Job role, department, performance ratings, satisfaction scores
  • Compensation & Benefits: Income, salary hikes, stock options, overtime status

docs.title: Target Variable Analysis
docs.text: Attrition Rate: 16% of employees in the dataset have left the organization, indicating a moderate but concerning attrition rate that aligns with industry averages for knowledge-based organizations.

docs.title: Data Quality Assessment
docs.text:
Strengths: - Complete Dataset: No missing values across all 2,940 records - Rich Feature Set: Comprehensive mix of categorical and numerical variables - Balanced Coverage: Good representation of different departments and job levels

Limitations: - Class Imbalance: 84% non-attrition vs 16% attrition creates modeling challenges - Unknown Variables: Some variables (DailyRate, HourlyRate, MonthlyRate) lack clear definitions - Potential Bias: Data from single organization may not generalize across industries

docs.title: Critical Variables Identified
docs.text:
Through initial analysis, several variables show immediate relevance:

  • OverTime: 28% of employees work overtime, significantly higher than industry norms
  • Job Satisfaction: 40% report low to medium-low satisfaction levels
  • Performance Ratings: Surprisingly, no employees rated below "Excellent" (potential data quality issue)

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2: Data Loading & Initial Exploration]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Analytical Framework
docs.text:
The EDA follows a structured approach to uncover attrition patterns:

  1. Univariate Analysis: Understanding individual variable distributions
  2. Bivariate Analysis: Relationship between each variable and attrition
  3. Multivariate Analysis: Complex interactions and correlations
  4. Business Context Integration: Translating statistical findings to actionable insights

docs.title: Key Findings from Numerical Variables
docs.text:
Age Distribution: - Near-normal distribution with mean age of 37 years - Good age diversity (18-60 years) indicates inclusive hiring practices - Attrition Insight: Younger employees show higher attrition rates

Income Analysis: - Mean monthly income: \(6,500 with high variance (\)1,000-$20,000) - Significant income inequality within organization - Critical Finding: Employees leaving earn 30% less than those staying

Experience Patterns: - Average company tenure: 7 years - Concerning Pattern: Employees leaving have 30% less total work experience - Promotion timing appears problematic (some employees 10+ years without promotion)

docs.title: Categorical Variable Insights
docs.text:
Department Analysis: - R&D: 65% of workforce, 14% attrition rate - Sales: 30% of workforce, 40% attrition rate (major concern) - HR: 5% of workforce, 25% attrition rate

Work-Life Balance Indicators: - Overtime Workers: 28% of employees, 30%+ attrition rate - Travel Requirements: Frequent travelers show 2x attrition rate - Distance from Home: Employees living farther attrite 16% more

docs.title: Statistical Significance
docs.text:
Strongest Predictors Identified: 1. Overtime status (odds ratio: 2.6x) 2. Monthly income (inverse relationship) 3. Job involvement levels 4. Work-life balance ratings 5. Years since last promotion

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3: Comprehensive EDA Implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Preprocessing Strategy
docs.text:
The preprocessing approach balances feature preservation with model requirements:

Variable Removal Decisions: - EmployeeNumber: Unique identifier with no predictive value - Over18: Single value variable (all employees over 18) - StandardHours: No variation across employees

docs.title: Feature Engineering Approach
docs.text:
Categorical Encoding: - One-Hot Encoding: Applied to multi-category variables (Department, JobRole, etc.) - Binary Mapping: Simple Yes/No variables converted to 1/0 - Ordinal Preservation: Satisfaction and involvement scales maintained as numerical

Feature Scaling Rationale: - Required for: Logistic Regression and SVM (distance-based algorithms) - Not Required for: Tree-based models (Decision Tree, Random Forest) - Method Used: StandardScaler (Z-score normalization)

docs.title: Train-Test Split Strategy
docs.text: 70-30 Split with Stratification: - Maintains 16% attrition rate in both training and test sets - Ensures model evaluation on representative data - Rationale: Prevents bias from uneven class distribution

docs.title: Preprocessing Limitations
docs.text:
Potential Issues: - Information Loss: One-hot encoding increases dimensionality - Multicollinearity: High correlations between experience-related variables - Feature Selection: No systematic feature selection applied

[See Code Walkthrough Section 4: Data Preprocessing Implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Algorithm Selection Rationale
docs.text:
Four algorithms were selected to cover different modeling approaches:

1. Logistic Regression - Strengths: Interpretable coefficients, probability outputs, baseline model - Use Case: Understanding feature relationships and establishing baseline performance

2. Support Vector Machine (SVM) - Linear Kernel: Tests linear separability assumption - RBF Kernel: Captures non-linear relationships - Use Case: Handling complex decision boundaries

3. Decision Tree - Strengths: Highly interpretable, handles non-linear relationships naturally - Weakness: Prone to overfitting - Use Case: Understanding decision pathways

4. Random Forest - Strengths: Reduces overfitting, feature importance, ensemble robustness - Use Case: Achieving best predictive performance

docs.title: Class Imbalance Handling
docs.text:
Challenge: 84% non-attrition vs 16% attrition creates bias toward majority class

Solution Applied: - Tree-based models: Class weights {0: 0.17, 1: 0.83} - Linear models: Threshold optimization using precision-recall curves

docs.title: Model Performance Summary
docs.text:
Logistic Regression (Optimized Threshold: 0.35): - Accuracy: 87% - Recall: 74% (significant improvement from 46% at default threshold) - Precision: 50% - Interpretation: Reasonable baseline with clear feature interpretation

SVM with RBF Kernel (Optimized Threshold: 0.35): - Accuracy: 88% - Recall: 82% (best among all models) - Precision: 52% - Interpretation: Best at identifying true attrition cases

Decision Tree (Default): - Training Performance: 100% (clear overfitting) - Test Recall: 80% - Test Precision: 73% - Interpretation: Overfits but provides interpretable rules

Random Forest (Default): - Training Performance: 100% (overfitting) - Test Recall: 80% - Test Precision: 75% - Interpretation: Best overall balance of metrics

docs.title: Critical Model Limitations
docs.text:
Overfitting Concerns: - Tree-based models show perfect training performance - Significant performance drop on test data - Risk: Models may not generalize to new employees

Precision-Recall Trade-off: - High recall comes at cost of precision - Business Impact: Many false positives means resources spent on employees not at risk

Feature Interpretation Challenges: - Random Forest feature importance may be unstable - Multicollinearity: Correlated features complicate interpretation

[See Code Walkthrough Section 5: Model Implementation & Training]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Evaluation Methodology
docs.text: Primary Metric: Recall for Attrition Class - Business Justification: Missing a departing employee is more costly than false alarms - Target: Maximize true positive identification while maintaining reasonable precision

docs.title: Threshold Optimization Process
docs.text: Precision-Recall Curve Analysis: - Optimal threshold identified at 0.35 for both Logistic Regression and SVM - Trade-off: Higher recall achieved by accepting lower precision - Business Context: Better to over-predict attrition than miss valuable departing employees

docs.title: Hyperparameter Tuning Results
docs.text:
Decision Tree Tuning: - Grid Search Parameters: max_depth, criterion, min_samples_leaf - Result: Tuned model reduces overfitting but sacrifices performance - Precision Drop: From 73% to 29% (concerning for business application)

Random Forest Tuning: - Grid Search Parameters: n_estimators, min_samples_leaf, max_features - Result: Slight improvement in recall with minimal precision loss - Best Performance: 82% recall, 76% precision on test data

docs.title: Feature Importance Analysis
docs.text:
Consistent Top Predictors Across Models: 1. OverTime: Strongest predictor across all models 2. MonthlyIncome: Inverse relationship with attrition 3. Age: Younger employees higher risk 4. TotalWorkingYears: Experience reduces attrition risk 5. DistanceFromHome: Longer commutes increase risk

Business Validation: - Feature rankings align with HR domain knowledge - Economic factors (income, overtime) dominate predictions - Work-life balance factors consistently important

docs.title: Model Selection Recommendation
docs.text:
For Production Use: Tuned Random Forest - Rationale: Best balance of recall (82%) and precision (76%) - Reliability: Ensemble method more robust than single models - Interpretability: Feature importance provides actionable insights

For Business Understanding: Logistic Regression - Rationale: Coefficient interpretation provides odds ratios - Transparency: Clear understanding of factor relationships - Baseline: Establishes performance floor for comparison

docs.title: Performance Limitations
docs.text:
Generalization Concerns: - Single organization data may not transfer to other companies - Industry-specific factors not captured - Temporal stability unknown (model may degrade over time)

Precision Challenges: - 24% false positive rate means significant resource waste - May cause employee morale issues if targeting becomes obvious - Cost-benefit analysis needed for implementation

[See Code Walkthrough Section 6: Model Evaluation & Tuning]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Primary Attrition Drivers
docs.text:
1. Overtime Work Culture (Strongest Predictor) - Finding: Employees working overtime are 2.6x more likely to leave - Business Impact: 28% of workforce affected - Recommendation: Implement workload management and compensation for overtime

2. Compensation Inequity - Finding: Departing employees earn 30% less than retained employees - Business Impact: Losing talent due to uncompetitive compensation - Recommendation: Conduct comprehensive salary benchmarking

3. Department-Specific Risks - Sales Department: 40% attrition rate (critical concern) - HR Department: 25% attrition rate - Recommendation: Develop department-specific retention strategies

docs.title: Strategic Recommendations
docs.text:
Immediate Actions (0-3 months):

  • Overtime Policy Review: Implement strict overtime limits with adequate compensation

  • Compensation Audit: Review salaries for bottom quartile performers

  • Sales Team Intervention: Immediate focus on sales department retention

Medium-term Initiatives (3-12 months):

  • Promotion Timeline Reform: Address 10+ year promotion gaps

  • Remote Work Options: Reduce commute burden for distant employees

  • Job Involvement Programs: Increase employee engagement initiatives

Long-term Strategic Changes (12+ months):

  • Culture Transformation: Address work-life balance systematically

  • Career Development: Clear promotion pathways and timelines

  • Stock Option Expansion: Broaden equity participation

docs.title: Implementation Framework
docs.text:
Targeted Intervention Strategy: 1. Model Scoring: Apply model monthly to identify at-risk employees 2. Risk Segmentation: High, medium, low risk categories 3. Intervention Mapping: Specific actions per risk level 4. Success Tracking: Monitor retention rates and intervention effectiveness

Resource Allocation Optimization: - High-Risk Employees: Immediate manager intervention, retention bonuses - Medium-Risk Employees: Career development discussions, workload review - Low-Risk Employees: Standard engagement activities

docs.title: Expected Business Outcomes
docs.text:
Cost Savings: - Estimated 30-40% reduction in retention spending through targeting - Reduced recruitment and training costs for high-value positions

Talent Retention: - 15-20% improvement in retention of identified at-risk employees - Reduced loss of institutional knowledge and client relationships

Operational Efficiency: - Proactive rather than reactive HR management - Data-driven decision making for HR investments

docs.title: Implementation Risks & Mitigation
docs.text:
Model Degradation Risk: - Issue: Model performance may decline over time - Mitigation: Quarterly model retraining and performance monitoring

Employee Privacy Concerns: - Issue: Predictive modeling may raise ethical questions - Mitigation: Transparent communication about model use and employee benefits

False Positive Costs: - Issue: 24% false positive rate creates unnecessary interventions - Mitigation: Graduated intervention approach, cost-benefit analysis

[See Code Walkthrough Section 7: Business Intelligence & Reporting]

# Calculate business impact metrics
def calculate_business_impact(recall, precision, total_employees=2940):
    """
    Calculate business impact of model deployment.

    Parameters:
    recall: Model recall rate
    precision: Model precision rate
    total_employees: Total employee count

    Returns:
    Dictionary with business impact metrics
    """
    # Assume 16% attrition rate
    actual_attrition = int(total_employees * 0.16)

    # Calculate model predictions
    true_positives = int(actual_attrition * recall)
    false_positives = int((true_positives / precision) - true_positives)
    false_negatives = actual_attrition - true_positives

    # Calculate intervention costs (example values)
    intervention_cost_per_employee = 5000  # Retention incentive cost
    missed_opportunity_cost = 25000  # Cost of losing valued employee

    # Calculate total costs
    intervention_costs = false_positives * intervention_cost_per_employee
    missed_opportunities = false_negatives * missed_opportunity_cost
    successful_retentions = true_positives * intervention_cost_per_employee

    return {
        'employees_correctly_identified': true_positives,
        'employees_incorrectly_targeted': false_positives,
        'employees_missed': false_negatives,
        'intervention_costs': intervention_costs,
        'missed_opportunity_costs': missed_opportunities,
        'retention_investment': successful_retentions,
        'total_cost': intervention_costs + missed_opportunities + successful_retentions
    }

# Example calculation for best model
best_model_impact = calculate_business_impact(recall=0.82, precision=0.76)
print("Business Impact Analysis:")
for key, value in best_model_impact.items():
    print(f"{key}: {value:,}")

def generate_attrition_report(model, X_data, feature_names, threshold=0.5):
    """
    Generate comprehensive attrition risk report for business stakeholders.

    Parameters:
    model: Trained model object
    X_data: Feature data for prediction
    feature_names: List of feature names for interpretation
    threshold: Classification threshold

    Returns:
    DataFrame with employee risk scores and recommendations
    """
    # Generate probability predictions
    if hasattr(model, 'predict_proba'):
        probabilities = model.predict_proba(X_data)[:, 1]
    else:
        # For models without probability output
        probabilities = model.decision_function(X_data)

    # Create risk categories
    def categorize_risk(prob):
        if prob >= 0.7:
            return 'High Risk'
        elif prob >= 0.4:
            return 'Medium Risk'
        else:
            return 'Low Risk'

    # Create report DataFrame
    report_df = pd.DataFrame({
        'employee_id': range(len(X_data)),
        'attrition_probability': probabilities,
        'risk_category': [categorize_risk(p) for p in probabilities],
        'predicted_attrition': probabilities > threshold
    })

    # Sort by risk level
    report_df = report_df.sort_values('attrition_probability', ascending=False)

    # Add recommendations
    def get_recommendation(risk_cat):
        recommendations = {
            'High Risk': 'Immediate manager intervention, retention bonus consideration',
            'Medium Risk': 'Career development discussion, workload review',
            'Low Risk': 'Standard engagement activities'
        }
        return recommendations[risk_cat]

    report_df['recommended_action'] = report_df['risk_category'].apply(get_recommendation)

    return report_df

# Example report generation

print(sample_report)

def model_performance_monitor(model, X_new, y_new, baseline_metrics):
    """
    Monitor model performance degradation over time.

    Parameters:
    model: Deployed model object
    X_new: New feature data
    y_new: New actual outcomes
    baseline_metrics: Dictionary of baseline performance metrics

    Returns:
    Performance comparison and alerts
    """
    # Generate new predictions
    y_pred_new = model.predict(X_new)

    # Calculate current metrics
    current_accuracy = metrics.accuracy_score(y_new, y_pred_new)
    current_recall = metrics.recall_score(y_new, y_pred_new)
    current_precision = metrics.precision_score(y_new, y_pred_new)

    # Compare with baseline
    accuracy_change = current_accuracy - baseline_metrics['accuracy']
    recall_change = current_recall - baseline_metrics['recall']
    precision_change = current_precision - baseline_metrics['precision']

    # Generate alerts
    alerts = []
    if accuracy_change < -0.05:
        alerts.append("ALERT: Accuracy decreased by more than 5%")
    if recall_change < -0.10:
        alerts.append("ALERT: Recall decreased by more than 10%")
    if precision_change < -0.10:
        alerts.append("ALERT: Precision decreased by more than 10%")

    monitoring_report = {
        'current_accuracy': current_accuracy,
        'current_recall': current_recall,
        'current_precision': current_precision,
        'accuracy_change': accuracy_change,
        'recall_change': recall_change,
        'precision_change': precision_change,
        'alerts': alerts,
        'recommendation': 'Model retraining recommended' if alerts else 'Model performing within acceptable range'
    }

    return monitoring_report

# Example baseline metrics
baseline = {'accuracy': 0.87, 'recall': 0.82, 'precision': 0.76}

docs.title: Scientific Foundation
docs.text:
This tutorial demonstrates machine learning applications in astronomy through multi-class classification of celestial objects. The objective is to distinguish between Stars, Galaxies, and Quasars using spectroscopic and photometric measurements from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS).

Astronomical Context:

Stars represent luminous plasma spheroids powered by nuclear fusion, with the Sun being our nearest example. The next closest star, Proxima Centauri, lies approximately 4.25 light-years away, illustrating the vast scales involved in astronomical observations.

Galaxies are gravitationally bound systems containing 10^8 to 10^14 stars, along with stellar remnants, interstellar gas, cosmic dust, and dark matter. These structures represent some of the largest organized matter formations in the observable universe.

Quasars (Quasi-stellar objects) are extremely luminous active galactic nuclei powered by supermassive black holes. Their defining characteristic is extreme redshift due to their tremendous distances from Earth, making them observable primarily in the early universe.

docs.title: The Redshift Phenomenon
docs.text:
Critical Insight: Redshift serves as the primary distinguishing feature for quasar identification. This phenomenon occurs because:

  1. Cosmological expansion causes electromagnetic radiation to lose energy over vast distances

  2. Doppler effect creates frequency shifts for objects receding at high velocities

  3. Distance-velocity relationship means more distant objects exhibit higher redshift values

This physical principle becomes the foundation for our machine learning approach, as algorithms can detect patterns in redshift measurements that correlate with object classifications.

docs.title: Problem Formulation
docs.text:
Supervised Classification Challenge: - Input: 17 numerical features from SDSS observations - Output: Categorical classification (Star=2, Galaxy=0, Quasar=1) - Dataset Scale: 250,000 observations with high astronomical data quality - Approach: Non-linear machine learning methods (k-NN and Decision Trees)

The problem represents a moderately imbalanced classification scenario with approximately 50% galaxies, 38% stars, and 12% quasars, reflecting the natural distribution of observable celestial objects.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 1: Environment Setup and Data Loading]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Data Source: Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS)
docs.text: The Sloan Digital Sky Survey represents one of astronomy's most comprehensive public datasets, utilizing a dedicated 2.5-meter wide-angle optical telescope at Apache Point Observatory, New Mexico. SDSS has catalogued over three million astronomical objects with both spectroscopic and photometric measurements.

docs.title: Feature Architecture Analysis
docs.text:
Spectroscopic Features (5 filters): - u, g, r, i, z: Ultraviolet through infrared photometric measurements - Physical significance: These represent energy emissions across the electromagnetic spectrum - Classification relevance: Different celestial objects exhibit characteristic spectral signatures

Positional Coordinates: - ra (Right Ascension), dec (Declination): Celestial positioning system - Impact on classification: Spatial distribution patterns may reveal object clustering

Technical Metadata: - run, rerun, camcol, field: Survey execution parameters - plate, mjd, fiberid: Observational setup identifiers - Preprocessing implication: These may require removal as non-predictive features

Critical Classification Feature: - redshift: Wavelength shift measurement - Astronomical importance: Primary indicator of cosmic distance and recession velocity - Expected model behavior: Should emerge as the most important predictive feature

docs.title: Data Quality Assessment
docs.text:
Exceptional Quality Characteristics: - Zero missing values: Professional astronomical data collection standards - No duplicate observations: Each celestial object uniquely identified - Large sample size: 250,000 observations provide robust statistical power - Balanced feature types: Entirely numerical features suitable for algorithmic processing

Sampling Strategy: For computational efficiency, the tutorial utilizes a 50,000-observation subsample while maintaining class proportions through stratified sampling. This approach preserves statistical relationships while enabling faster iteration during model development.

docs.title: Class Distribution Analysis
docs.text:
Natural Imbalance Reflection: - Galaxies (50.3%): Most abundant observable objects at current survey sensitivity - Stars (38.2%): Limited to Milky Way objects visible from Earth - Quasars (11.5%): Rare, distant objects requiring sensitive detection methods

This distribution reflects astronomical reality rather than sampling bias, making it an authentic representation of observable celestial object frequencies.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 2: Data Loading and Initial Exploration]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Statistical Distribution Patterns
docs.text:
Key Distribution Characteristics:

Right-Skewed Variables: - redshift, plate, field, dec: Exhibit long tails toward higher values - Astronomical interpretation: Reflects survey design and cosmic object distribution - Modeling implication: May benefit from logarithmic transformation for certain algorithms

Symmetric Distributions: - Photometric filters (u, g, r, i, z): Near-normal distributions - Physical significance: Represents natural variation in stellar brightness measurements - Model advantage: Well-suited for distance-based algorithms without transformation

docs.title: Univariate Analysis Insights
docs.text:
Redshift Distribution: The redshift variable shows extreme right skew with values ranging from near-zero to 6.4. This wide range corresponds to objects from nearby (within our galaxy) to cosmologically distant (early universe). The log-transformation reveals more interpretable patterns, with distinct peaks corresponding to different object classes.

Photometric Filter Analysis: The five photometric filters (u, g, r, i, z) demonstrate correlated but distinct distributions. High correlations between adjacent wavelength bands (g-r: 0.85, r-i: 0.87) reflect the continuous nature of electromagnetic spectra while maintaining independent information for classification.

docs.title: Class-Specific Distribution Patterns
docs.text:
Redshift as Primary Discriminator: - Stars: Extremely low redshift (z ≈ 0), indicating galactic proximity - Galaxies: Moderate redshift distribution reflecting various cosmic distances - Quasars: High redshift tail extending to z > 6, confirming cosmological distances

Photometric Signatures: Each celestial object type exhibits characteristic spectral patterns: - Stars: Relatively consistent brightness across filters - Galaxies: Complex multi-component light profiles - Quasars: Often point-source appearance with unique spectral features

docs.title: Correlation Structure Analysis
docs.text:
High Positive Correlations (>0.8): - Adjacent photometric bands: Physical proximity in electromagnetic spectrum - mjd-plate correlation: Survey execution temporal clustering - Implication: Potential for dimensionality reduction while preserving information

Notable Negative Correlations: - redshift-class relationship: Higher redshift values associate with quasar classification - Strategic importance: Confirms astronomical theory through data-driven discovery

docs.title: Feature Engineering Decisions
docs.text:
Metadata Variable Assessment: Through distribution analysis, several technical variables showed minimal class discrimination: - rerun: Single unique value (constant) - run, field, fiberid, camcol: Uniform distributions across classes - Decision: Remove non-predictive technical metadata - Retention criteria: Keep variables showing class-specific patterns

Dimensionality Optimization: Original 17 features reduced to 10 predictive features by removing: 1. Unique identifiers: objid, specobjid 2. Technical constants: rerun 3. Survey metadata: run, field, fiberid, camcol

This preprocessing maintains astronomical information while eliminating technical artifacts.

[See Code Walkthrough Section 3: Comprehensive EDA Implementation]

↩ Back to Top

docs.title: Label Encoding Strategy
docs.text:
Target Variable Transformation: The categorical target variable undergoes label encoding for algorithmic compatibility: - Galaxy → 0 - Quasar → 1 - Star → 2

Rationale: This numerical encoding preserves class relationships without imposing artificial ordinality, making it suitable for both distance-based and tree-based algorithms.

docs.title: Train-Test Split Methodology
docs.text:
Stratified Sampling Approach: - Split ratio: 90% training, 10% testing - Stratification: Maintains original class proportions in both sets - Random state: Fixed for reproducibility - Result: 45,000 training observations, 5,000 test observations

Why Stratification Matters: Given the natural class imbalance (especially the smaller quasar class), stratified sampling ensures adequate representation of all celestial object types in both training and validation sets.

docs.title: Feature Scaling Considerations
docs.text:
Algorithm-Specific Requirements:

k-Nearest Neighbors: - Scaling necessity: High - distance calculations sensitive to feature magnitude differences - Method: StandardScaler normalization (mean=0, std=1) - Impact: Dramatic performance improvement observed

Decision Trees: - Scaling necessity: Low - tree splits based on threshold comparisons, not distances - Observation: Minimal performance change with/without scaling - Computational benefit: Can skip scaling step for tree-based models

docs.title: Dimensionality Reduction Analysis
docs.text:
Principal Component Analysis (PCA) Evaluation:

For k-NN with PCA: - Implementation: Full PCA transformation after standardization - Performance impact: Varies depending on variance retention - Computational trade-off: Reduced feature space vs. information loss

Best Practice: Test PCA impact empirically rather than assuming benefit, as astronomical data often contains meaningful signal across all measured wavelengths.

docs.text:

Feature distribution assessment: Outliers identified but retained (astronomical extremes often meaningful) 4. Class balance verification: Proportions maintained through stratification

Feature Selection Outcomes: - Initial features: 17 total - After ID removal: 15 predictive candidates - After metadata filtering: 10 core astronomical measurements - Retention criteria: Class discrimination capability and astronomical relevance

docs.title: Algorithm Selection Rationale
docs.text:
k-Nearest Neighbors (k-NN): - Strength: Captures local patterns in high-dimensional space - Astronomical relevance: Similar objects should cluster in feature space - Non-parametric advantage: No assumptions about underlying data distribution - Computational consideration: Scales poorly with large datasets

Decision Trees: - Strength: Hierarchical decision-making mirrors astronomical classification logic - Interpretability: Clear feature importance and decision pathways - Non-linear capability: Handles complex feature interactions - Efficiency: Computationally scalable for large astronomical datasets

docs.title: k-NN Performance Analysis
docs.text:
Without Preprocessing: - Training Accuracy: Moderate performance - Test Accuracy: Declining performance indicating overfitting - Issue: Different feature scales dominate distance calculations

With Scaling and PCA: - Standardization impact: Significant improvement in classification metrics - PCA considerations: May reduce performance if important spectral information is compressed - Optimal configuration: StandardScaler + selective PCA retention

Performance Metrics Interpretation: - Precision by class: Varies significantly across celestial object types - Recall patterns: Stars and galaxies generally easier to classify than quasars - F1-scores: Balanced measure showing overall classification effectiveness

docs.title: Decision Tree Performance Analysis
docs.text:
Unscaled Performance: - Training Results: High accuracy (>95%) - Test Results: Strong generalization (>90%) - Class-specific performance: Excellent discrimination across all celestial types

Scaled Performance: - Observation: Minimal change confirms scale-invariance of tree algorithms - Implication: Preprocessing overhead unnecessary for tree-based methods - Consistency: Both scaled and unscaled versions achieve similar results

docs.title: Feature Importance Revelations
docs.text:
Redshift Dominance: The decision tree analysis reveals redshift as the overwhelmingly important feature (>70% importance), confirming astronomical theory: - Physical basis: Redshift directly correlates with cosmic distance - Classification logic: Distant objects (high redshift) are typically quasars - Tree structure: Redshift forms the root node split

Secondary Features: - Photometric filters: Provide complementary spectral signature information - Positional coordinates: Minor contribution to classification accuracy - Technical metadata: Negligible importance (correctly filtered out)

docs.title: Cross-Validation Assessment
docs.text:
5-Fold Cross-Validation Results: - Decision Tree: Consistent performance across folds (>90% average) - Stability metric: Low variance between fold performances - Generalization confidence: High reliability for unseen astronomical data

Overfitting Analysis: - Training vs. Test gap: Minimal for Decision Trees - k-NN concern: Higher overfitting tendency, especially without proper preprocessing - Mitigation strategy: Hyperparameter tuning and regularization

docs.title: Algorithm Comparison Summary
docs.text:
Decision Tree Advantages: 1. Superior accuracy: >90% on test set 2. Computational efficiency: Fast training and prediction 3. Interpretability: Clear decision pathways 4. Scale invariance: No preprocessing overhead 5. Astronomical insight: Confirms redshift importance

k-NN Limitations: 1. Preprocessing dependence: Requires careful scaling 2. Computational cost: Increases with dataset size 3. Performance ceiling: Lower maximum accuracy achieved 4. Memory requirements: Stores entire training set

docs.title: Comprehensive Metrics Analysis
docs.text:
Classification Report Interpretation:

Decision Tree Results: - Overall Accuracy: 92-95% across training and test sets - Precision by Class: - Galaxy: >95% (abundant training data) - Star: >90% (clear spectral signatures) - Quasar: >85% (challenging due to rarity) - Recall Patterns: Consistent high recall across all classes - F1-Score Balance: >90% for all celestial object types

Confusion Matrix Insights: - Primary confusion: Minor misclassification between galaxies and quasars - Star classification: Nearly perfect separation from other classes - Physical interpretation: Confusion aligns with astronomical transition zones

docs.title: Cross-Validation Methodology
docs.text:
5-Fold Stratified Cross-Validation: - Fold consistency: 89-92% accuracy range - Mean performance: 90.5% ± 1.2% - Standard deviation: Low variance indicates robust model - Implication: High confidence in generalization to new astronomical surveys

Why K-Fold Validation Matters: Given the astronomical data's natural clustering (objects from same sky regions), cross-validation ensures the model performs well across different survey areas and observation conditions.

docs.title: Performance Comparison Context
docs.text:
Baseline Performance Expectations: - Random classification: 33% accuracy (three classes) - Majority class baseline: 50% (always predict galaxy) - Our achievement: 90%+ represents substantial improvement over naive approaches

Real-World Performance Standards: - Astronomical survey requirements: >90% accuracy for automated classification - Manual classification time: Hours per object for human astronomers - Model efficiency: Milliseconds per classification with comparable accuracy

docs.title: Computational Performance Analysis
docs.text:
Training Time Comparison: - Decision Tree: <5 seconds on 45,000 observations - k-NN: <2 seconds (no explicit training phase) - Prediction Time: - Decision Tree: ~0.1ms per object - k-NN: ~1-5ms per object (distance calculations)

Scalability Assessment: - Dataset growth impact: Decision Trees scale logarithmically - k-NN scaling: Linear with training set size (problematic for large surveys) - Memory requirements: Decision Trees store compact rule sets vs. k-NN's full training data

docs.title: Error Analysis and Failure Modes
docs.text:
Systematic Misclassification Patterns: 1. Galaxy-Quasar confusion: Objects with intermediate redshift values 2. Star outliers: Stars with unusual spectral properties 3. Survey edge cases: Objects near detection limits

Physical Interpretation of Errors: Many misclassifications occur at astronomical transition boundaries: - Active galaxies with quasar-like properties - Nearby galaxies with star-like point sources - Variable stars with changing brightness patterns

Model Reliability Zones: - High confidence: Clear redshift separation (z<0.1 stars, z>2 quasars) - Moderate confidence: Intermediate redshift galaxies - Challenging cases: Objects with ambiguous spectral signatures

docs.title: Performance Optimization Opportunities
docs.text:
Hyperparameter Tuning Potential: - Decision Tree depth: Balance between accuracy and interpretability - k-NN k-value: Optimize for local neighborhood structure - Feature selection: Focus on most discriminative measurements

Ensemble Method Prospects: - Random Forest: Multiple tree combination for improved robustness - Gradient boosting: Sequential error correction for edge cases - Voting classifiers: Combine k-NN and tree predictions

docs.title: Model Strengths and Astronomical Validation
docs.text:
Decision Tree Success Factors:

1. Redshift-Driven Classification: The model's primary reliance on redshift for classification aligns perfectly with astronomical theory. The hierarchical decision structure naturally separates: - Local objects (z ≈ 0): Stars within our galaxy - Intermediate redshift (0.1 < z < 2): Nearby to moderate-distance galaxies - High redshift (z > 2): Distant quasars from the early universe

2. Spectral Signature Recognition: Secondary splits on photometric filters (u, g, r, i, z) capture genuine astrophysical differences: - Stellar spectra: Characteristic blackbody patterns - Galaxy composites: Mixed stellar population signatures - Quasar activity: Active galactic nucleus emission lines

3. Domain Knowledge Emergence: The model discovers astronomical principles without explicit programming: - Distance-luminosity relationships - Spectral type correlations - Cosmological redshift patterns

docs.title: Model Limitations and Failure Modes
docs.text:
1. Edge Case Challenges: - Low-redshift quasars: Rare nearby active galaxies may be misclassified - Point-source galaxies: Distant galaxies appearing star-like - Variable objects: Time-varying brightness complicates classification

2. Survey-Specific Bias: - SDSS wavelength range: Limited to optical/near-infrared observations - Magnitude limits: Faint object selection bias - Sky coverage: Northern hemisphere preference

3. Temporal Considerations: - Static snapshots: No time-series information for variable objects - Survey epoch effects: Observational conditions impact measurements - Instrument calibration: Systematic measurement variations

docs.text:

def extended_statistics(df):
    """Calculate extended statistical measures for numerical columns."""
    stats = {}
    for col in df.select_dtypes(include=[np.number]).columns:
        stats[col] = {
            'mean': df[col].mean(),
            'median': df[col].median(),
            'mode': df[col].mode().iloc[0] if not df[col].mode().empty else np.nan,
            'std': df[col].std(),
            'skewness': df[col].skew(),
            'kurtosis': df[col].kurtosis(),
            'range': df[col].max() - df[col].min(),
            'iqr': df[col].quantile(0.75) - df[col].quantile(0.25)
        }
    return pd.DataFrame(stats).T

extended_stats = extended_statistics(df_astro)
print("\nExtended Statistics:")
print(extended_stats)

def hist_box(col):
    """
    Create combined histogram and boxplot for univariate analysis.

    Parameters:
    col (str): Column name to analyze

    Returns:
    None: Displays combined plot
    """
    f, (ax_box, ax_hist) = plt.subplots(2, sharex=True, 
                                       gridspec_kw={'height_ratios': (0.15, 0.85)}, 
                                       figsize=(15, 10))
    sns.set(style='darkgrid')

    # Boxplot for outlier detection
    sns.boxplot(x=df_astro[col], ax=ax_box, showmeans=True, color='skyblue')

    # Histogram with KDE for distribution analysis
    sns.histplot(df_astro[col], kde=True, ax=ax_hist, stat='density', 
                color='skyblue', fill=True)
    sns.kdeplot(df_astro[col], ax=ax_hist, color='blue', linestyle='-')

    # Add mean and median lines
    ax_hist.axvline(df_astro[col].mean(), color='green', linestyle='--', 
                   label=f'Mean: {df_astro[col].mean():.2f}')
    ax_hist.axvline(df_astro[col].median(), color='orange', linestyle='-', 
                   label=f'Median: {df_astro[col].median():.2f}')

    ax_hist.legend()
    plt.title(f'Distribution Analysis: {col}')
    plt.show()

Purpose: Provide comprehensive univariate analysis combining distribution shape, central tendency, and outlier detection.

Flow: 1. Subplot creation: Combined layout for boxplot and histogram 2. Boxplot generation: Outlier identification and quartile visualization 3. Histogram creation: Distribution shape with kernel density estimation 4. Statistical overlay: Mean and median lines for central tendency

Impact: This function enables systematic analysis of all numerical features. Removing components reduces analytical depth and pattern detection capability.

def plot_class_distributions(column):
    """
    Plot distributions for each astronomical object class.

    Parameters:
    column (str): Column name to analyze by class

    Returns:
    None: Displays class-specific distribution plot
    """
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))

    # Plot distribution for each class
    for class_label in df_astro['class'].unique():
        class_data = df_astro[df_astro['class'] == class_label][column]
        sns.kdeplot(data=class_data, label=f'{class_label}', alpha=0.7)

    # Add overall distribution
    sns.kdeplot(data=df_astro[column], label='Overall', color='black', linestyle='--')

    plt.xlabel(column)
    plt.ylabel('Density')
    plt.title(f'Distribution of {column} by Astronomical Object Class')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
    plt.show()

    # Statistical summary by class
    class_stats = df_astro.groupby('class')[column].describe()
    print(f"\nStatistical summary for {column} by class:")
    print(class_stats)

def feature_selection_analysis():
    """
    Analyze features for removal based on uniqueness and discrimination.

    Returns:
    list: Features recommended for removal
    """
    features_to_remove = []

    # Check for constant features
    for col in df_astro.columns:
        if col != 'class' and df_astro[col].nunique() == 1:
            features_to_remove.append(col)
            print(f"Constant feature detected: {col}")

    # Check for identifier columns
    identifier_columns = ['objid', 'specobjid']
    for col in identifier_columns:
        if col in df_astro.columns:
            features_to_remove.append(col)
            print(f"Identifier column: {col}")

    # Analyze discrimination power for technical features
    technical_features = ['run', 'field', 'fiberid', 'camcol', 'rerun']

    for feature in technical_features:
        if feature in df_astro.columns:
            # Calculate class-wise distributions
            class_distributions = df_astro.groupby('class')[feature].apply(
                lambda x: x.value_counts(normalize=True)
            ).unstack(fill_value=0)

            # Simple discrimination test: check if distributions are similar
            discrimination_score = class_distributions.var(axis=0).mean()

            if discrimination_score < 0.01:  # Low discrimination threshold
                features_to_remove.append(feature)
                print(f"Low discrimination feature: {feature} (score: {discrimination_score:.4f})")

    return features_to_remove

# Identify features for removal
removal_candidates = feature_selection_analysis()

# Remove identified features
print(f"\nRemoving {len(removal_candidates)} features: {removal_candidates}")
df_astro = df_astro.drop(columns=removal_candidates, errors='ignore')

print(f"Dataset shape after feature removal: {df_astro.shape}")
print(f"Remaining features: {df_astro.columns.tolist()}")

Purpose: Remove non-predictive features to improve model efficiency and reduce overfitting risk.

Flow: 1. Constant detection: Identify features with single unique value 2. Identifier removal: Drop unique ID columns without predictive value 3. Discrimination analysis: Assess technical features for class separation ability 4. Systematic removal: Clean dataset of non-informative features

Impact: Feature removal reduces computational overhead and potential overfitting. Removing important features degrades model performance.

def create_train_test_split():
    """
    Create stratified train-test split maintaining class proportions.

    Returns:
    tuple: X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test splits
    """
    # Separate features and target
    feature_columns = [col for col in df_astro.columns if col != 'class']

    # Stratified split to maintain class proportions
    X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
        X, y, 
        test_size=0.1,           # 90% train, 10% test
        random_state=42,         # Reproducibility
        stratify=y               # Maintain class proportions
    )

    print(f"\nTrain set shapes: X_train {X_train.shape}, y_train {y_train.shape}")
    print(f"Test set shapes: X_test {X_test.shape}, y_test {y_test.shape}")

    # Verify stratification worked
    print("\nClass distribution in training set:")
    print(y_train.value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index())
    print("\nClass distribution in test set:")
    print(y_test.value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index())

def implement_pca_analysis():
    """
    Implement Principal Component Analysis for dimensionality reduction.

    Returns:
    dict: PCA results and transformed datasets
    """
    from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

    # Full PCA to analyze variance explained
    pca_full = PCA()
    X_train_pca_full = pca_full.fit_transform(scaled_data['standard']['X_train'])

    # Analyze explained variance
    explained_variance_ratio = pca_full.explained_variance_ratio_
    cumulative_variance = np.cumsum(explained_variance_ratio)

    print("PCA Variance Analysis:")
    for i, (individual, cumulative) in enumerate(zip(explained_variance_ratio, cumulative_variance)):
        print(f"PC{i+1}: {individual:.4f} individual, {cumulative:.4f} cumulative")

    # Plot explained variance
    plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))

    plt.subplot(1, 2, 1)
    plt.bar(range(1, len(explained_variance_ratio) + 1), explained_variance_ratio)
    plt.xlabel('Principal Component')
    plt.ylabel('Explained Variance Ratio')
    plt.title('Individual Explained Variance by Component')

    plt.subplot(1, 2, 2)
    plt.plot(range(1, len(cumulative_variance) + 1), cumulative_variance, 'bo-')
    plt.axhline(y=0.95, color='r', linestyle='--', label='95% Variance')
    plt.xlabel('Number of Components')
    plt.ylabel('Cumulative Explained Variance')
    plt.title('Cumulative Explained Variance')
    plt.legend()
    plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    # Determine optimal number of components for 95% variance
    n_components_95 = np.argmax(cumulative_variance >= 0.95) + 1
    print(f"\nComponents needed for 95% variance: {n_components_95}")

    # Apply PCA with optimal components
    pca_optimal = PCA(n_components=n_components_95)
    X_train_pca = pca_optimal.fit_transform(scaled_data['standard']['X_train'])
    X_test_pca = pca_optimal.transform(scaled_data['standard']['X_test'])

    print(f"Original feature space: {scaled_data['standard']['X_train'].shape[1]} dimensions")
    print(f"Reduced feature space: {X_train_pca.shape[1]} dimensions")
    print(f"Variance retained: {cumulative_variance[n_components_95-1]:.4f}")

    return {
        'pca_full': pca_full,
        'pca_optimal': pca_optimal,
        'X_train_pca': X_train_pca,
        'X_test_pca': X_test_pca,
        'n_components': n_components_95,
        'variance_explained': cumulative_variance[n_components_95-1]
    }

# Execute PCA analysis
pca_results = implement_pca_analysis()

Purpose: Reduce feature dimensionality while preserving maximum information content for computational efficiency.

Impact: PCA reduces computational cost and potential overfitting but may remove astronomically meaningful information. Balance efficiency with interpretability.

def metrics_score(actual, predicted, class_names=None):
    """
    Comprehensive model evaluation with multiple metrics.

    Parameters:
    actual (array-like): True class labels
    predicted (array-like): Predicted class labels
    class_names (list): Optional class names for labeling

    Returns:
    None: Prints metrics and displays confusion matrix
    """
    if class_names is None:
        class_names = ['Galaxy', 'Quasar', 'Star']

    # Print classification report
    print("Classification Report:")
    print(classification_report(actual, predicted, target_names=class_names))

    # Create and display confusion matrix
    cm = confusion_matrix(actual, predicted)

    plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=True, fmt='d', cmap='Blues',
                xticklabels=class_names, yticklabels=class_names)
    plt.ylabel('Actual Class')
    plt.xlabel('Predicted Class')
    plt.title('Confusion Matrix')
    plt.show()

    # Additional metrics
    from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

    accuracy = accuracy_score(actual, predicted)
    precision = precision_score(actual, predicted, average='weighted')
    recall = recall_score(actual, predicted, average='weighted')
    f1 = f1_score(actual, predicted, average='weighted')

    print(f"\nOverall Metrics:")
    print(f"Accuracy: {accuracy:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted Precision: {precision:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted Recall: {recall:.4f}")
    print(f"Weighted F1-Score: {f1:.4f}")

    return {
        'accuracy': accuracy,
        'precision': precision,
        'recall': recall,
        'f1_score': f1,
        'confusion_matrix': cm
    }

Purpose: Provide comprehensive model evaluation with multiple performance metrics and visualization.

Flow: 1. Classification report: Per-class precision, recall, F1-score 2. Confusion matrix: Visual representation of classification errors 3. Overall metrics: Weighted averages for imbalanced classes 4. Return results: Structured output for comparison

Impact: Comprehensive evaluation reveals model strengths and weaknesses. Missing metrics can hide important performance issues.

        'KNN_Optimized': knn_results['optimized']['model'],
        'DT_Basic': DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42),
        'DT_Optimized': dt_results['optimized']['model']
    }

    # Data configurations
    data_configs = {
        'Raw': (X_train, X_test),
        'Scaled': (scaled_data['standard']['X_train'], scaled_data['standard']['X_test']),
        'PCA': (pca_results['X_train_pca'], pca_results['X_test_pca'])
    }

    print("=== Comprehensive Cross-Validation Results ===")

    for model_name, model in models.items():
        cv_results[model_name] = {}

        for data_name, (X_tr, X_te) in data_configs.items():
            try:
                # Perform cross-validation
                scores = cross_val_score(model, X_tr, y_train, cv=cv_strategy, 
                                       scoring='accuracy', n_jobs=-1)

                cv_results[model_name][data_name] = {
                    'mean_score': scores.mean(),
                    'std_score': scores.std(),
                    'scores': scores
                }

                print(f"{model_name} - {data_name}: "
                      f"{scores.mean():.4f} ± {scores.std():.4f}")

            except Exception as e:
                print(f"Error with {model_name} - {data_name}: {str(e)}")
                cv_results[model_name][data_name] = None

    # Create visualization of cross-validation results
    plt.figure(figsize=(15, 8))

    model_names = []
    mean_scores = []
    std_scores = []

    for model_name in models.keys():
        for data_name in data_configs.keys():
            if (model_name in cv_results and 
                data_name in cv_results[model_name] and 
                cv_results[model_name][data_name] is not None):

                model_names.append(f"{model_name}_{data_name}")
                mean_scores.append(cv_results[model_name][data_name]['mean_score'])
                std_scores.append(cv_results[model_name][data_name]['std_score'])

    x_pos = np.arange(len(model_names))
    plt.bar(x_pos, mean_scores, yerr=std_scores, capsize=5, alpha=0.7)

def advanced_performance_analysis():
    """
    Conduct detailed performance analysis including learning curves and error analysis.

    Returns:
    dict: Comprehensive performance analysis results
    """
    from sklearn.model_selection import learning_curve, validation_curve

    analysis_results = {}

    # Select best performing models
    best_knn = knn_results['optimized']['model']
    best_dt = dt_results['optimized']['model']

    # Learning curve analysis
    print("=== Learning Curve Analysis ===")

    def plot_learning_curve(model, X, y, title, scoring='accuracy'):
        """Plot learning curves for given model."""
        train_sizes, train_scores, val_scores = learning_curve(
            model, X, y, cv=5, n_jobs=-1, 
            train_sizes=np.linspace(0.1, 1.0, 10),
            scoring=scoring, random_state=42
        )

        train_mean = np.mean(train_scores, axis=1)
        train_std = np.std(train_scores, axis=1)
        val_mean = np.mean(val_scores, axis=1)
        val_std = np.std(val_scores, axis=1)

        plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
        plt.plot(train_sizes, train_mean, 'o-', label='Training Score', alpha=0.8)
        plt.fill_between(train_sizes, train_mean - train_std, train_mean + train_std, alpha=0.2)

        plt.plot(train_sizes, val_mean, 'o-', label='Validation Score', alpha=0.8)
        plt.fill_between(train_sizes, val_mean - val_std, val_mean + val_std, alpha=0.2)

        plt.xlabel('Training Set Size')
        plt.ylabel('Accuracy Score')
        plt.title(f'Learning Curve: {title}')
        plt.legend()
        plt.grid(True, alpha=0.3)
        plt.show()

        return {
            'train_sizes': train_sizes,
            'train_scores': train_scores,
            'val_scores': val_scores
        }

    # Generate learning curves
    analysis_results['knn_learning'] = plot_learning_curve(
        best_knn, pca_results['X_train_pca'], y_train, 'k-NN Classifier'
    )

    analysis_results['dt_learning'] = plot_learning_curve(

def detailed_error_analysis():
    """
    Perform detailed analysis of model errors and misclassification patterns.

    Returns:
    dict: Error analysis results and insights
    """
    error_results = {}

    # Use best performing model (Decision Tree)
    best_model = dt_results['optimized']['model']
    predictions = best_model.predict(X_test)

    # Create detailed error analysis
    error_mask = y_test != predictions
    correct_mask = y_test == predictions

    print("=== Error Analysis ===")
    print(f"Total test samples: {len(y_test)}")
    print(f"Correct predictions: {correct_mask.sum()}")
    print(f"Incorrect predictions: {error_mask.sum()}")
    print(f"Error rate: {error_mask.mean():.4f}")

    # Analyze errors by true class
    error_by_class = {}
    class_names = ['Galaxy', 'Quasar', 'Star']

    for class_idx, class_name in enumerate(class_names):
        class_mask = y_test == class_idx
        class_errors = error_mask & class_mask

        error_by_class[class_name] = {
            'total_samples': class_mask.sum(),
            'errors': class_errors.sum(),
            'error_rate': class_errors.sum() / class_mask.sum() if class_mask.sum() > 0 else 0
        }

        print(f"\n{class_name} errors:")
        print(f"  Total samples: {class_mask.sum()}")
        print(f"  Errors: {class_errors.sum()}")
        print(f"  Error rate: {error_by_class[class_name]['error_rate']:.4f}")

    # Analyze confusion patterns
    print("\n=== Confusion Pattern Analysis ===")
    cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, predictions)

    # Most common misclassifications
    misclassifications = []
    for true_class in range(3):
        for pred_class in range(3):
            if true_class != pred_class and cm[true_class, pred_class] > 0:
                misclassifications.append({
                    'true_class': class_names[true_class],
                    'predicted_class': class_names[pred_class],
                    'count': cm[true_class, pred_class],
                    'percentage': cm[true_class, pred_class] / cm[true_class].sum() * 100
                })

    misclassifications.sort(key=lambda x: x['count'], reverse=True)

    print("Most common misclassifications:")
    for misc in misclassifications[:5]:
        print(f"  {misc['true_class']} → {misc['predicted_class']}: "
              f"{misc['count']} cases ({misc['percentage']:.2f}%)")

    # Feature importance in errors
    if hasattr(best_model, 'feature_importances_'):
        feature_names = X_train.columns
        importances = best_model.feature_importances_

        # Create feature importance plot
        plt.figure(figsize=(12, 8))
        indices = np.argsort(importances)[::-1]

        plt.bar(range(len(importances)), importances[indices])
        plt.xticks(range(len(importances)), [feature_names[i] for i in indices], rotation=45)
        plt.xlabel('Features')
        plt.ylabel('Importance')
        plt.title('Feature Importance in Decision Tree Model')
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.show()

        error_results['feature_importance'] = {
            'features': feature_names,
            'importances': importances,
            'sorted_indices': indices
        }

    error_results['error_by_class'] = error_by_class
    error_results['misclassifications'] = misclassifications
    error_results['confusion_matrix'] = cm

    return error_results

# Execute detailed error analysis
error_analysis = detailed_error_analysis()

def production_readiness_assessment():
    """
    Assess model readiness for production deployment in astronomical surveys.

    Returns:
    dict: Production readiness metrics and recommendations
    """
    # Select best model for assessment
    best_model = dt_results['optimized']['model']

    assessment = {
        'performance_metrics': {},
        'computational_metrics': {},
        'robustness_metrics': {},
        'interpretability_metrics': {},
        'recommendations': []
    }

    # Performance thresholds for astronomical applications
    performance_thresholds = {
        'accuracy': 0.90,      # 90% accuracy minimum
        'precision': 0.85,     # 85% precision minimum
        'recall': 0.85,        # 85% recall minimum
        'f1_score': 0.85       # 85% F1-score minimum
    }

    test_metrics = dt_results['optimized']['test_metrics']

    print("=== Production Readiness Assessment ===")
    print("\n1. Performance Requirements:")

    for metric, threshold in performance_thresholds.items():
        actual_value = test_metrics[metric]
        meets_requirement = actual_value >= threshold
        status = "✓ PASS" if meets_requirement else "✗ FAIL"

        print(f"   {metric.capitalize()}: {actual_value:.4f} >= {threshold} {status}")
        assessment['performance_metrics'][metric] = {
            'value': actual_value,
            'threshold': threshold,
            'meets_requirement': meets_requirement
        }

    # Computational efficiency assessment
    print("\n2. Computational Efficiency:")

    import time

    # Measure prediction time
    start_time = time.time()
    predictions = best_model.predict(X_test)
    prediction_time = time.time() - start_time
    predictions_per_second = len(X_test) / prediction_time

    print(f"   Prediction time: {prediction_time:.4f} seconds for {len(X_test)} objects")
    print(f"   Throughput: {predictions_per_second:.0f} objects/second")

    # Memory usage assessment
    import sys
    model_size = sys.getsizeof(best_model) / 1024  # KB
    print(f"   Model size: {model_size:.2f} KB")

    assessment['computational_metrics'] = {
        'prediction_time': prediction_time,
        'throughput': predictions_per_second,
        'model_size_kb': model_size
    }

    # Robustness assessment
    print("\n3. Robustness Assessment:")

    # Cross-validation stability
    cv_scores = cv_results.get('DT_Optimized', {}).get('Raw', {}).get('scores', [])
    if cv_scores:
        cv_std = np.std(cv_scores)
        print(f"   Cross-validation stability: {cv_std:.4f} (std dev)")
        assessment['robustness_metrics']['cv_stability'] = cv_std

    # Class balance handling
    class_f1_scores = []
    for class_idx in range(3):
        class_mask = y_test == class_idx
        if class_mask.sum() > 0:
            class_pred = predictions[class_mask]
            class_true = y_test[class_mask]
            class_f1 = f1_score(class_true, class_pred, average='binary', 
                               pos_label=class_idx, zero_division=0)
            class_f1_scores.append(class_f1)

    min_class_f1 = min(class_f1_scores) if class_f1_scores else 0
    print(f"   Minimum class F1-score: {min_class_f1:.4f}")
    assessment['robustness_metrics']['min_class_f1'] = min_class_f1

    # Interpretability assessment
    print("\n4. Interpretability:")

    if hasattr(best_model, 'feature_importances_'):
        top_feature_importance = np.max(best_model.feature_importances_)
        print(f"   Top feature importance: {top_feature_importance:.4f}")
        print(f"   Model type: Decision Tree (highly interpretable)")
        assessment['interpretability_metrics'] = {
            'top_feature_importance': top_feature_importance,
            'interpretable': True,
            'explanation_available': True
        }

    # Generate recommendations
    print("\n5. Deployment Recommendations:")

    recommendations = []

    # Performance-based recommendations
    overall_performance = all(assessment['performance_metrics'][m]['meets_requirement'] 
                            for m in performance_thresholds.keys())

    if overall_performance:
        recommendations.append("✓ Model meets all performance requirements for production")
    else:
        recommendations.append("⚠ Model requires performance improvement before production")

    # Efficiency recommendations
    if predictions_per_second > 1000:
        recommendations.append("✓ Computational efficiency suitable for real-time processing")
    else:
        recommendations.append("⚠ Consider optimization for high-throughput applications")

    # Robustness recommendations
    if cv_std < 0.02:
        recommendations.append("✓ Model shows good stability across validation folds")
    else:
        recommendations.append("⚠ Model stability could be improved with more regularization")

    # Domain-specific recommendations
    recommendations.extend([
        "✓ Decision tree structure aligns with astronomical classification logic",
        "✓ Redshift importance matches astrophysical theory",
        "✓ Model provides interpretable decision pathways for astronomers",
        "⚠ Consider ensemble methods for mission-critical applications",
        "⚠ Implement confidence scoring for uncertain classifications"
    ])

    for rec in recommendations:
        print(f"   {rec}")

    assessment['recommendations'] = recommendations

    return assessment

# Execute production readiness assessment
production_assessment = production_readiness_assessment()

def class_specific_performance_analysis():
    """
    Perform detailed analysis of model performance for each astronomical object class.

    Returns:
    dict: Class-specific performance metrics and insights
    """
    best_model = dt_results['optimized']['model']
    predictions = best_model.predict(X_test)

    class_names = ['Galaxy', 'Quasar', 'Star']
    class_analysis = {}

    print("=== Class-Specific Performance Analysis ===")

    for class_idx, class_name in enumerate(class_names):
        print(f"\n{class_name} Analysis:")

        # Get samples for this class
        class_mask = y_test == class_idx
        class_true = y_test[class_mask]
        class_pred = predictions[class_mask]

        if len(class_true) == 0:
            print(f"  No samples found for {class_name}")
            continue

        # Calculate class-specific metrics
        class_accuracy = accuracy_score(class_true, class_pred)
        class_precision = precision_score(y_test, predictions, labels=[class_idx], 
                                        average=None, zero_division=0)[0]
        class_recall = recall_score(y_test, predictions, labels=[class_idx], 
                                  average=None, zero_division=0)[0]
        class_f1 = f1_score(y_test, predictions, labels=[class_idx], 
                           average=None, zero_division=0)[0]

        print(f"  Sample count: {len(class_true)}")
        print(f"  Accuracy: {class_accuracy:.4f}")
        print(f"  Precision: {class_precision:.4f}")
        print(f"  Recall: {class_recall:.4f}")
        print(f"  F1-Score: {class_f1:.4f}")

        # Analyze misclassifications
        misclassified = class_true != class_pred
        misclassification_rate = misclassified.sum() / len(class_true)

        print(f"  Misclassification rate: {misclassification_rate:.4f}")

        if misclassified.sum() > 0:
            misclassified_as = class_pred[misclassified]
            for target_class in range(3):
                if target_class != class_idx:
                    target_count = (misclassified_as == target_class).sum()
                    if target_count > 0:
                        target_rate = target_count / misclassified.sum()
                        print(f"    {target_count} misclassified as {class_names[target_class]} "
                              f"({target_rate:.2%} of errors)")

        # Feature importance for this class
        if hasattr(best_model, 'feature_importances_'):
            # Get samples correctly classified for this class
            correctly_classified = (y_test == class_idx) & (predictions == class_idx)

            if correctly_classified.sum() > 10:  # Ensure sufficient samples
                # Analyze feature values for correctly classified instances
                correct_features = X_test[correctly_classified]
                feature_means = correct_features.mean()
                feature_stds = correct_features.std()

                print(f"  Characteristic feature values (correctly classified):")
                important_features = np.argsort(best_model.feature_importances_)[-3:][::-1]

                for feat_idx in important_features:
                    feat_name = X_test.columns[feat_idx]
                    feat_mean = feature_means.iloc[feat_idx]
                    feat_std = feature_stds.iloc[feat_idx]
                    print(f"    {feat_name}: {feat_mean:.3f} ± {feat_std:.3f}")

        class_analysis[class_name] = {
            'sample_count': len(class_true),
            'accuracy': class_accuracy,
            'precision': class_precision,
            'recall': class_recall,
            'f1_score': class_f1,
            'misclassification_rate': misclassification_rate
        }

    # Create class-specific performance visualization
    metrics = ['precision', 'recall', 'f1_score']
    class_names_list = list(class_analysis.keys())

    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

    for i, metric in enumerate(metrics):
        metric_values = [class_analysis[cls][metric] for cls in class_names_list]

        bars = axes[i].bar(class_names_list, metric_values, alpha=0.7, 
                          color=['skyblue', 'lightcoral', 'lightgreen'])
        axes[i].set_ylabel(metric.capitalize())
        axes[i].set_title(f'{metric.capitalize()} by Class')
        axes[i].set_ylim(0, 1)
        axes[i].grid(True, alpha=0.3)

        # Add value labels on bars
        for bar, value in zip(bars, metric_values):
            axes[i].text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width()/2, bar.get_height() + 0.01,
                        f'{value:.3f}', ha='center', va='bottom')

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

    return class_analysis

        'spatial_distribution': {},
        'domain_validation': {}
    }

    print("=== Astronomical Insights from Machine Learning Model ===")

    # 1. Redshift Analysis
    print("\n1. Redshift Analysis:")

    if 'redshift' in feature_names:
        redshift_importance = best_model.feature_importances_[feature_names.index('redshift')]
        print(f"   Redshift feature importance: {redshift_importance:.4f}")

        # Analyze redshift distributions by class
        for class_idx, class_name in enumerate(['Galaxy', 'Quasar', 'Star']):
            class_mask = y_test == class_idx
            if class_mask.sum() > 0:
                class_redshift = X_test[class_mask]['redshift']
                redshift_stats = {
                    'mean': class_redshift.mean(),
                    'std': class_redshift.std(),
                    'median': class_redshift.median(),
                    'min': class_redshift.min(),
                    'max': class_redshift.max()
                }

                print(f"   {class_name} redshift: mean={redshift_stats['mean']:.3f}, "
                      f"std={redshift_stats['std']:.3f}, "
                      f"range=[{redshift_stats['min']:.3f}, {redshift_stats['max']:.3f}]")

                insights['redshift_analysis'][class_name] = redshift_stats

        # Redshift-based classification boundaries
        print("\n   Redshift Classification Insights:")
        print("   - Stars: Very low redshift (z ≈ 0) - local galactic objects")
        print("   - Galaxies: Moderate redshift range - various cosmic distances")
        print("   - Quasars: High redshift values - distant early universe objects")

    # 2. Photometric Pattern Analysis
    print("\n2. Photometric Filter Analysis:")

    photometric_filters = ['u', 'g', 'r', 'i', 'z']
    available_filters = [f for f in photometric_filters if f in feature_names]

    if available_filters:
        filter_importances = {}
        for filter_name in available_filters:
            filter_idx = feature_names.index(filter_name)
            filter_importances[filter_name] = best_model.feature_importances_[filter_idx]

        # Sort by importance
        sorted_filters = sorted(filter_importances.items(), key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True)

        print("   Filter importance ranking:")
        for filter_name, importance in sorted_filters:
            print(f"   {filter_name}: {importance:.4f}")

        insights['photometric_patterns']['filter_importance'] = filter_importances

        # Analyze color indices (astronomical standard)
        color_indices = {}
        if 'g' in available_filters and 'r' in available_filters:
            X_test_copy = X_test.copy()
            X_test_copy['g_r_color'] = X_test_copy['g'] - X_test_copy['r']

            for class_idx, class_name in enumerate(['Galaxy', 'Quasar', 'Star']):
                class_mask = y_test == class_idx
                if class_mask.sum() > 0:
                    class_color = X_test_copy[class_mask]['g_r_color']
                    color_indices[class_name] = {
                        'g_r_mean': class_color.mean(),
                        'g_r_std': class_color.std()
                    }

            print("\n   Color Index Analysis (g-r):")
            for class_name, color_data in color_indices.items():
                print(f"   {class_name}: g-r = {color_data['g_r_mean']:.3f} ± {color_data['g_r_std']:.3f}")

            insights['photometric_patterns']['color_indices'] = color_indices

    # 3. Spatial Distribution Analysis
    print("\n3. Spatial Distribution Analysis:")

    spatial_features = ['ra', 'dec']
    available_spatial = [f for f in spatial_features if f in feature_names]

    if available_spatial:
        spatial_importances = {}
        for coord in available_spatial:
            coord_idx = feature_names.index(coord)
            spatial_importances[coord] = best_model.feature_importances_[coord_idx]

        print("   Coordinate importance:")
        for coord, importance in spatial_importances.items():
            print(f"   {coord}: {importance:.4f}")

        if spatial_importances['ra'] < 0.05 and spatial_importances['dec'] < 0.05:
            print("   → Low spatial importance suggests objects are distributed uniformly")
            print("   → Classification primarily based on intrinsic properties, not position")

        insights['spatial_distribution']['coordinate_importance'] = spatial_importances

    # 4. Domain Knowledge Validation
    print("\n4. Domain Knowledge Validation:")

    validation_results = []

    # Check if redshift is the most important feature
    if 'redshift' in feature_names:
        redshift_idx = feature_names.index('redshift')
        redshift_importance = best_model.feature_importances_[redshift_idx]
        most_important = np.argmax(best_model.feature_importances_) == redshift_idx

        if most_important:
            validation_results.append("✓ Redshift identified as most important feature (matches theory)")
        else:
            validation_results.append("⚠ Redshift not most important (unexpected)")

        insights['domain_validation']['redshift_primary'] = most_important

    # Check photometric filter correlations
    if len(available_filters) >= 3:
        validation_results.append("✓ Multiple photometric filters used (spectral analysis)")
        insights['domain_validation']['multi_wavelength'] = True

    # Check spatial feature importance
    if all(f in feature_names for f in ['ra', 'dec']):
        spatial_importance_total = (best_model.feature_importances_[feature_names.index('ra')] + 
                                  best_model.feature_importances_[feature_names.index('dec')])

        if spatial_importance_total < 0.1:
            validation_results.append("✓ Low spatial dependence (intrinsic classification)")
            insights['domain_validation']['position_independent'] = True
        else:
            validation_results.append("⚠ High spatial dependence (potential survey bias)")
            insights['domain_validation']['position_independent'] = False

    print("   Domain Validation Results:")
    for result in validation_results:
        print(f"   {result}")

    # 5. Scientific Interpretation
    print("\n5. Scientific Interpretation:")
    print("   The machine learning model has discovered several key astronomical principles:")
    print("   - Redshift as primary distance/recession indicator")
    print("   - Spectral signatures distinguish object types")
    print("   - Position-independent intrinsic property classification")
    print("   - Hierarchical decision structure mirrors astronomical taxonomy")

    return insights

# Execute astronomical insights analysis
astronomical_insights = astronomical_insights_analysis()

Purpose: Extract and validate astronomical insights from the machine learning model to confirm alignment with established astrophysical principles.

Flow: 1. Redshift analysis: Examine the role of cosmological distance measurements 2. Photometric patterns: Analyze spectral signature importance 3. Spatial distribution: Assess position-dependence of classification 4. Domain validation: Compare model insights with astronomical theory 5. Scientific interpretation: Translate technical results to astronomical knowledge

Impact: Domain validation confirms that the machine learning model has discovered genuine astronomical relationships, validating both the model and the underlying physical principles.
